How to choose astronomy software by task: sky maps, observation planning, satellite tracking, telescope control, image processing, data exploration and citizen science.

Astronomy software can help you identify objects, plan observations, control equipment, process images and explore scientific data. The best tool depends on whether you are standing outside with a phone, planning a telescope session or analysing astrophotography.

This guide is organised by **task**, not by product. Start with what you want to do tonight, pick one tool that does it well, and add others only when a real need appears. Most people need far less software than the internet suggests.

## Sky maps and planetariums

A sky map answers the question "what am I looking at, and what else is up there?" For most beginners it is the only software they need.

- **Desktop planetarium software.** Programs such as Stellarium, KStars and Cartes du Ciel simulate the sky for any place and time. Stellarium is the most beginner-friendly of the three, while KStars and Cartes du Ciel add features useful to telescope users. Desktop tools are best for planning and for learning how the sky moves. [source: check each project's site for platforms and licences]
- **Mobile sky maps.** Phone apps use your device's sensors to show the sky where you point it. They are convenient outdoors, but sensors can be inaccurate (especially compass readings), and screens ruin dark adaptation unless there is a night mode. Look for a red-light setting and lower the brightness.
- **Browser-based planetariums.** A web version needs no installation and works on almost any device, which suits classrooms and quick checks. It usually needs an internet connection and offers fewer features than the desktop version.
- **Location and time settings.** The most common mistake is a wrong location or time. Check both, and check the time zone and daylight-saving setting, before deciding that something is missing.
- **Offline access.** If you observe from a dark site with poor mobile signal, choose software that works offline, and download what you need in advance, including catalogues and any orbital data for satellites.

## Observation planning

Planning turns "I hope to see something" into a productive evening.

- **Object visibility.** Check whether an object will be above the horizon, in a dark enough sky and clear of the Moon during your observing window.
- **Altitude and azimuth.** Altitude is how high an object is above the horizon, and azimuth is its compass direction. Objects low down are dimmer and blurrier because you look through more atmosphere. As a rough guide, aim to observe targets well above the horizon.
- **Rise and set times.** These tell you when to start and stop. Remember that times depend on your location and that the horizon may be blocked by buildings or trees.
- **Moon illumination.** The Moon's phase and position affect how well you see faint objects. A bright Moon near the target is the biggest single enemy of deep-sky observing.
- **Dark-sky planning.** Combine a light-pollution map, a cloud and transparency forecast, and the Moon's schedule. A service that forecasts cloud, such as Clear Outside, is a useful companion for this step. [source: verify current service]
- **Exporting observing lists.** Many planetariums let you build a list of targets and export it, so you can print it, load it onto a phone or send it to a telescope-control program. Keep lists short: six well-chosen targets beat thirty rushed ones.

## Satellite tracking

Watching a satellite cross the sky is one of the easiest and most rewarding beginner activities.

- **ISS passes.** The International Space Station is often the brightest moving object in the sky. Websites and apps such as NASA's Spot the Station and Heavens-Above list passes for your location. [source: verify current services]
- **Bright satellite predictions.** Some satellites brighten briefly at particular angles, and prediction tools list these for your location.
- **TLE data.** Predictions rely on orbital element sets, often called two-line elements (TLEs), published by organisations such as CelesTrak. Software converts these into predicted positions. Make sure the data is recent. [source: CelesTrak]
- **Limitations of long-range predictions.** Satellites are pushed off course by atmospheric drag and by deliberate manoeuvres, such as reboosts of the ISS. Predictions made days ahead can shift, and predictions made weeks ahead are unreliable. Check again on the day.
- **Why satellite visibility can change.** For a satellite to be visible, it needs to be lit by the Sun while you are in darkness. That is why passes cluster after dusk and before dawn. Weather, horizon obstructions and the satellite's changing orientation also change what you see. Newly launched groups of satellites can appear as a "train" and then spread out and fade as they raise their orbits.

## Telescope control

If you have a computerised telescope, software can find and track objects for you.

- **Go-to mounts.** A go-to mount points at a chosen object after you have aligned it. Many can be controlled from a computer or handset.
- **ASCOM or INDI compatibility.** ASCOM is a widely used standard for astronomy hardware on Windows. INDI is an open protocol used on Linux, macOS and other systems. Software that supports the standard your equipment uses will save you trouble. Programs that commonly support these standards include KStars with its Ekos suite, Cartes du Ciel and N.I.N.A. [source: verify each tool's supported platforms and standards]
- **Alignment.** Even the best software depends on a good alignment. Follow your mount's procedure carefully, and make sure the date, time and location are correct.
- **Remote observing.** You can control equipment from indoors or from another location. Remote setups add cables, power, network reliability and safety considerations, so start with a simple local system first.
- **Hardware compatibility.** Check that your mount, camera and focuser have drivers that work with the software and your operating system before you buy either. Compatibility problems are a more common cause of frustration than software features.

## Astrophotography processing

Processing turns a set of faint, noisy exposures into a finished image. The steps are similar across tools.

- **Calibration frames.** Dark, flat and bias frames record the camera's noise, dust shadows and vignetting so they can be removed. Taking them properly matters more than any later trick.
- **Stacking.** Combining many exposures increases signal relative to noise. Free tools such as Siril and DeepSkyStacker are popular choices; other packages are paid. For planets and the Moon, tools such as AutoStakkert! are commonly used to stack video frames. [source: verify current tools and licences]
- **Stretching.** Raw astronomical data looks dark because most signal lies in a narrow range of brightness. A non-linear stretch reveals faint detail. Over-stretching brightens noise, so work gradually.
- **Noise reduction.** Reduce noise carefully. Aggressive settings can smear real detail and produce a plastic look.
- **Colour and gradient correction.** Light pollution and the Moon create colour casts and brightness gradients across a frame. Gradient-removal tools help. Colour calibration should aim for realistic star colours unless you are deliberately using false colour.
- **Responsible image presentation.** Say how an image was made. Note whether it is a single exposure or a stack, whether colours are natural or false-colour (as in narrowband palettes), and whether tools that generate or sharpen detail were used. Do not add detail that the data does not contain, and do not present composites as single photographs. Honest captions make your work more credible, not less.

## Astronomical data

Professional astronomy shares its data openly, and much of it is available to anyone.

- **Image archives.** Archives from major observatories and missions host images and observations. The ESA and NASA archives, and the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes (MAST), include data from missions such as Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope. [source: verify current archives and access]
- **Catalogue browsers.** Tools such as SIMBAD, VizieR and Aladin (from the CDS in Strasbourg) let you look up objects, overlay catalogues on sky images and compare data. [source: CDS]
- **FITS files.** FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) is the standard file format for astronomical images and tables. It stores the data plus a header describing how the data was taken and where it points. Viewers such as SAOImageDS9 and Python libraries such as Astropy can open them. [source: verify tools]
- **Planetary data.** NASA's JPL Horizons system provides positions for planets, moons, asteroids and comets. Mission archives hold images and measurements from spacecraft. [source: verify]
- **Earth-observation data.** Copernicus Sentinel data can be browsed through platforms such as the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem and explored with tools like ESA's SNAP toolbox or QGIS. This links directly to our [Earth observation section](/earth-observation/). [source: verify]
- **Coordinate systems.** Right ascension and declination locate objects on the celestial sphere in the same way longitude and latitude do on Earth. Altitude and azimuth describe where something is from your location at a particular time. Galactic coordinates are used for objects in the Milky Way. Always check which system and reference frame (for example, J2000 or ICRS) a tool uses.

## Citizen science

Citizen science lets you contribute to real research, sometimes with nothing more than a web browser.

- **Galaxy classification.** Projects on the Zooniverse platform, such as Galaxy Zoo, ask volunteers to classify galaxy shapes. [source: verify current project status]
- **Variable stars.** The American Association of Variable Star Observers (AAVSO) collects brightness estimates from amateurs worldwide and provides guidance and tools. [source: AAVSO]
- **Exoplanet transit analysis.** Some projects analyse the small dips in a star's brightness caused by a planet passing in front of it. NASA's Exoplanet Watch is one example. [source: verify current status]
- **Solar observation.** Some projects involve counting sunspots or classifying solar images. Use only safe methods, such as online images or properly filtered equipment, and never look at the Sun directly through unfiltered optics.
- **Asteroid search.** Volunteers help find and confirm moving objects in survey images. Look for projects that provide their own image sets and instructions. [source: verify specific project]

Project availability changes. Check that a project is active before investing time in it. See our [citizen science section](/citizen-science/) for more.

## How to evaluate software

Ask these questions before you commit time, money or data to any tool:

- **Cost.** Is it free, a one-off purchase, or a subscription? Is the free version enough for your needs?
- **Licence.** "Free" can mean free to use, open source, or free with limits. Check what you may do with your images and data.
- **Platform.** Does it run on your operating system and device?
- **Open-source status.** Open-source software can be inspected, adapted and often outlives commercial products. It is not automatically better, but it is often more transparent.
- **Offline capability.** Will it work at a dark site without a signal?
- **Privacy.** What location, device or account data does it collect? Does it need an account? Read the permissions before granting them.
- **Update frequency.** Is it actively maintained? A tool that has not been updated for years may not work with current operating systems or hardware.
- **Documentation.** Good documentation and an active user community save hours.
- **Hardware compatibility.** Confirm that it supports your specific mount, camera and other devices before buying either.

How to choose binoculars for stargazing: what the numbers mean, which sizes suit which observers, when a tripod helps and what binoculars can and cannot show.

<!-- Route: /resources/binoculars/ (add a matching route or move to /journal/ until then) -->

Binoculars are often the best first optical instrument for astronomy: they are portable, relatively easy to use and provide a wide field of view. A good pair can reveal lunar detail, star clusters, bright nebulae and some galaxies.

NASA highlights binoculars as a practical first observing instrument and gives 7×35 to 10×50 as useful general ranges. The Royal Astronomical Society commonly recommends 8×40 or 10×50, while warning that larger and heavier binoculars become difficult to hold steadily. [source: NASA; source: Royal Astronomical Society; verify wording and links before publishing]

The most important point in this guide is that the biggest, most magnifying or most expensive pair is not automatically the best. The best binoculars are the ones you will carry outside, hold steadily and enjoy using.

## Understand the numbers

Every pair of binoculars is marked with two numbers, for example **8×42**.

- **First number: magnification.** An 8× pair makes objects look eight times closer. Higher magnification shows more detail, but it also magnifies every tremor of your hands, narrows the field of view and makes the image dimmer for a given lens size.
- **Second number: objective-lens diameter.** This is the width of the front lenses in millimetres. Bigger lenses collect more light, which helps with faint objects, but they also add weight and cost.
- **Exit pupil.** Divide the objective diameter by the magnification. An 8×42 pair has an exit pupil of about 5.3 mm; a 10×50 has 5 mm; a 7×50 has about 7 mm. This is the width of the beam of light leaving the eyepiece. If it is larger than your own pupil at night, some light is wasted. Young, dark-adapted eyes may open to around 7 mm, while older eyes usually open less, so an exit pupil of 5 mm or so suits most people well. [source: verify pupil sizes]
- **Field of view.** This is how much sky you see at once. It is usually given either in degrees or as a width in metres at 1,000 metres (one degree is roughly 17.5 metres at 1,000 metres). A wide field makes it easier to find objects and better shows large targets such as star clusters. As a guide, the Pleiades cluster spans roughly 2 degrees of sky. Check the specification for the exact figure for any model.
- **Eye relief.** This is the distance from the eyepiece at which your eye can see the whole field. If you wear glasses, look for long eye relief (many people suggest around 15 mm or more) and eyecups that fold down. [source: verify recommended value]

## Useful astronomy sizes

- **7×35: light and wide-field.** Easy to hold, forgiving and good for sweeping across the Milky Way. A sensible choice for younger observers, for travel or if you want something you will grab on impulse.
- **8×40 or 8×42: versatile and comfortable.** A very good all-round size. Bright enough for most sky objects, steady enough to hold for a few minutes and usable in daylight for birdwatching too. For many beginners, this is the sweet spot.
- **10×50: brighter and more detailed, but harder to hold steadily.** Shows more stars and finer lunar detail than smaller binoculars. It is heavier, though, and most people find the image shakes noticeably after a minute or two. Leaning on a wall, car roof or a reclining chair helps.
- **15×70 and larger: specialist use, usually requiring support.** These reveal more star clusters and faint objects but are heavy and nearly impossible to hold steadily by hand for long. Treat them as a second pair, used with a tripod or mount, rather than a first purchase.

## What to prioritise

Specifications tell only part of the story. When you compare models, look for:

- **Optical quality.** A sharp, contrasty image matters more than an extra few millimetres of aperture. Cheap binoculars can show colour fringes around bright objects and blur toward the edges. Fully multi-coated lenses and good prisms (often labelled BaK4) usually help. Hold the binoculars at arm's length and look at the exit pupils: they should be round and bright, not squared-off or grey at the edges. [source: verify prism and coating guidance]
- **Collimation.** This means the two halves are properly aligned. Poor alignment gives double images or eyestrain, and hard knocks can throw good binoculars out of alignment.
- **Comfortable focusing.** A smooth, firm focus wheel and a dioptre adjustment for the difference between your eyes make a large difference over a whole evening.
- **Eye relief for glasses wearers.** See above. If you have to press your glasses against the eyepiece to see the full field, the binoculars will annoy you.
- **Weight.** If they feel heavy in the shop, they will feel heavier after twenty minutes of looking up. Heavier binoculars are also harder to hold steady.
- **Weather resistance.** Look for water-resistant or waterproof construction, and sealed or nitrogen-filled models if you observe in damp or cold weather. Fogging inside the tubes is a nuisance and can be a sign of poor sealing.
- **Warranty and repairability.** A longer warranty and a manufacturer that can repair or realign binoculars are worth more than a small saving.

## When to use a tripod

Hand-holding is fine for casual sky-sweeping, but support helps in several situations:

- **High magnification.** Above about 10×, most people struggle to keep the image steady.
- **Long observing sessions.** Arms tire quickly when pointing upward.
- **Detailed lunar observation.** Craters and mountain shadows are much easier to study on a steady image.
- **Older or less steady observers.** A support can make observing comfortable rather than frustrating.
- **Larger 15×70 or 20×80 binoculars.** These are designed to be mounted.

Many binoculars have a threaded socket under the hinge cover for a tripod adapter. A sturdy camera tripod with a simple L-shaped bracket or a dedicated binocular mount will do the job. If you do not want a tripod, try lying back in a reclining chair and resting your elbows on the arms. This makes a surprising difference.

Image-stabilised binoculars are another option. They steady the view electronically but cost considerably more and can be heavier. They are best considered as a later upgrade.

## What binoculars can show

Under reasonable skies, even a small pair reveals far more than the naked eye.

- **The Moon.** Craters, dark plains (maria) and mountain ranges. Look along the terminator for the best detail. Around new Moon, you may also see earthshine on the dark part of the disc.
- **The Pleiades.** Dozens of stars instead of the six or so visible without help. Their wide field suits binoculars perfectly.
- **The Hyades.** A large V-shaped cluster in Taurus, too spread out for most telescopes but ideal for binoculars.
- **The Orion Nebula.** A soft, misty glow around the middle "star" of Orion's sword, with a few stars embedded in it.
- **The Andromeda Galaxy.** A faint, elongated smudge of light under dark skies. It will not look like a photograph, but seeing light that has travelled for millions of years is a milestone.
- **Star fields.** The Milky Way resolves into countless faint stars, especially in Cygnus, Cassiopeia and towards Sagittarius on summer and autumn nights.
- **Bright comets.** When one appears, binoculars are often the best way to see the coma and tail. Check current predictions from reliable sources, as brightness is difficult to forecast. [source: BAA comet section]
- **Some open clusters.** Objects such as the Double Cluster in Perseus and the Beehive Cluster (M44) in Cancer are highlights.
- **Jupiter's moons.** Steadily held binoculars can show up to four tiny points of light beside Jupiter, changing position from night to night.

## What binoculars cannot do well

Being honest about limitations will save you disappointment.

- **Resolve fine planetary detail.** Jupiter and Saturn appear as small discs or points. You will not see cloud bands clearly or Saturn's rings in detail.
- **Show faint galaxies from bright urban skies.** Light pollution washes out faint objects, and binoculars gather less light than a telescope of similar cost.
- **Replace a telescope for high magnification.** For close-up views of the planets, tight double stars or small nebulae, you need a telescope.
- **Make every object visually dramatic.** Most deep-sky objects look like grey smudges to the eye. The pleasure lies in knowing what you are looking at and finding it yourself.

## Buying checklist

- **Try them before buying if possible.** A local astronomical society or an independent optics shop lets you compare weight, focus feel and comfort. Numbers cannot capture that.
- **Check both eyes focus correctly.** Cover one eyepiece at a time and confirm each side gives a sharp image once the dioptre adjustment is set.
- **Inspect stars near the edge of the field.** Some blur at the edges is normal, but stars that smear badly or show strong colour fringes suggest poor optics.
- **Look for duplicated or distorted images.** Double vision or a persistent strain in your eyes can point to poor alignment.
- **Check the exit pupils.** They should be round and clean when you hold the binoculars away from your eyes.
- **Avoid buying purely based on magnification.** A well-made 8×42 usually shows more than a poorly made 12×50.
- **Consider a used pair.** Good used binoculars can be excellent value, but test them carefully and check alignment.

## Safe solar observing

This is the most important safety section in the guide.

- **Never look at the Sun through binoculars.** Focused sunlight can cause permanent eye damage in a fraction of a second, and you may not feel any pain until it is too late.
- **Do not improvise front-mounted filters.** Sunglasses, smoked glass, exposed film, CDs and similar items are not safe.
- **Be very cautious about projection.** Projecting the Sun's image through binoculars onto a card is sometimes described, but it is risky: the optics can overheat and be damaged, and one careless moment of looking through them is dangerous. We do not recommend it for beginners, and a pinhole projector or a safe solar viewer is a far better introduction.
- **For serious solar viewing, use equipment designed and certified for solar observation.** This means solar filters made for the front of the binoculars or a purpose-built solar instrument, following the manufacturer's instructions and checking that any filter is undamaged and secure before every use.

The Royal Astronomical Society warns that binoculars and telescopes must never be used for direct solar viewing without appropriate protection. [source: Royal Astronomical Society; verify wording]

Binoculars are often the best first optical instrument for astronomy: they are portable, relatively easy to use and provide a wide field of view. A good pair can reveal lunar detail, star clusters, bright nebulae and some galaxies.

NASA highlights binoculars as a practical first observing instrument and gives 7×35 to 10×50 as useful general ranges. The most important point in this guide is that the biggest, most magnifying or most expensive pair is not automatically the best. The best binoculars are the ones you will carry outside, hold steadily and enjoy using.

Understand the numbers

Every pair of binoculars is marked with two numbers, for example 8×42.

  • First number: magnification. An 8× pair makes objects look eight times closer. Higher magnification shows more detail, but it also magnifies every tremor of your hands, narrows the field of view and makes the image dimmer for a given lens size.
  • Second number: objective-lens diameter. This is the width of the front lenses in millimetres. Bigger lenses collect more light, which helps with faint objects, but they also add weight and cost.
  • Exit pupil. Divide the objective diameter by the magnification. An 8×42 pair has an exit pupil of about 5.3 mm; a 10×50 has 5 mm; a 7×50 has about 7 mm. This is the width of the beam of light leaving the eyepiece. If it is larger than your own pupil at night, some light is wasted. Young, dark-adapted eyes may open to around 7 mm, while older eyes usually open less, so an exit pupil of 5 mm or so suits most people well. [source: verify pupil sizes]
  • Field of view. This is how much sky you see at once. It is usually given either in degrees or as a width in metres at 1,000 metres (one degree is roughly 17.5 metres at 1,000 metres). A wide field makes it easier to find objects and better shows large targets such as star clusters. As a guide, the Pleiades cluster spans roughly 2 degrees of sky. Check the specification for the exact figure for any model.
  • Eye relief. This is the distance from the eyepiece at which your eye can see the whole field. If you wear glasses, look for long eye relief (many people suggest around 15 mm or more) and eyecups that fold down. [source: verify recommended value]

  • 10×50: brighter and more detailed, but harder to hold steadily. Shows more stars and finer lunar detail than smaller binoculars. It is heavier, though, and most people find the image shakes noticeably after a minute or two. Leaning on a wall, car roof or a reclining chair helps.
  • 15×70 and larger: specialist use, usually requiring support. These reveal more star clusters and faint objects but are heavy and nearly impossible to hold steadily by hand for long. Treat them as a second pair, used with a tripod or mount, rather than a first purchase.

What to prioritise

Specifications tell only part of the story. When you compare models, look for:

  • Optical quality. A sharp, contrasty image matters more than an extra few millimetres of aperture. Cheap binoculars can show colour fringes around bright objects and blur toward the edges. Fully multi-coated lenses and good prisms (often labelled BaK4) usually help. Hold the binoculars at arm’s length and look at the exit pupils: they should be round and bright, not squared-off or grey at the edges. [source: verify prism and coating guidance]
  • Collimation. This means the two halves are properly aligned. Poor alignment gives double images or eyestrain, and hard knocks can throw good binoculars out of alignment.
  • Comfortable focusing. A smooth, firm focus wheel and a dioptre adjustment for the difference between your eyes make a large difference over a whole evening.
  • Eye relief for glasses wearers. See above. If you have to press your glasses against the eyepiece to see the full field, the binoculars will annoy you.
  • Weight. If they feel heavy in the shop, they will feel heavier after twenty minutes of looking up. Heavier binoculars are also harder to hold steady.
  • Weather resistance. Look for water-resistant or waterproof construction, and sealed or nitrogen-filled models if you observe in damp or cold weather. Fogging inside the tubes is a nuisance and can be a sign of poor sealing.
  • Warranty and repairability. A longer warranty and a manufacturer that can repair or realign binoculars are worth more than a small saving.

SEO for space organisations in 2026: what actually works now
A practical guide to SEO for space organisations, covering topical authority, structured content, AI search, and technical best practices.
A satellite orbiting Earth representing space sector search engine optimisation

## Why space SEO is different

Space organisations often publish technically accurate content that is hard for non-specialists to find. That creates a gap between what the organisation knows and what users can actually discover through search. Good SEO bridges that gap by connecting mission pages, research outputs, funding calls, services, and educational content into one coherent, discoverable ecosystem.

Search intent in the sector is mixed. A user might want mission updates, a journalist might want a quote, a student might want a plain-English explanation, and a procurement lead might want technical specifications. A strong SEO strategy maps each of those intents to a different page type instead of forcing everything into a single blog feed.

## What works now

In 2026, the most effective approach is to build topical authority around a small number of recurring themes. For a space organisation, those themes might be Earth observation, satellite communications, launch services, planetary science, space policy, STEM outreach, or climate applications. Search engines reward content ecosystems that show depth, consistency, and clear internal relationships between pages.

<ComparisonTable
  leftTitle="Old SEO"
  rightTitle="2026 SEO"
  rows={[
    { left: "Target broad keywords.", right: "Build topical authority around clear themes." },
    { left: "Hide detail in PDFs.", right: "Publish discoverable web pages with structured data." },
    { left: "Write for search engines first.", right: "Write for users, AI summaries, and search engines together." }
  ]}
/>

The second pillar is entity clarity. Search systems increasingly understand organisations, people, missions, instruments, locations, and projects as connected entities. Your site should make those relationships explicit through structured headings, metadata, author pages, and schema. This helps both classic SEO and AI-driven search experiences.

The third pillar is speed and technical cleanliness. Space organisations often have visually rich pages, but heavy, poorly structured, or inaccessible pages lose ranking potential and user trust. Fast loading, mobile-friendly layouts, semantic HTML, and accessible media are foundational, not optional.

## Content that wins

The best-performing content tends to be practical, specific, and audience-led. For space organisations, that usually means:

- Mission explainers
- Data portals and usage guides
- FAQs and glossary pages
- Careers and pathways content
- Case studies and impact stories
- Funding and procurement guidance
- Research summaries written for different expertise levels

Broad news content still has a place, but it works best when supported by evergreen explainers that can rank consistently over time.

In 2026, content should also be written to answer a question completely enough that it can surface in AI summaries or featured answers. That means concise lead paragraphs, strong definitions, bullet lists, and clear takeaways. Search visibility increasingly rewards pages that are easy to quote accurately.

<Checklist
  title="Technical checklist"
  items={[
    "Clear page titles and meta descriptions for every mission, project, and service page.",
    "Structured data for organisations, articles, events, videos, and FAQs where relevant.",
    "Logical heading structure and internal linking between related topics.",
    "Fast performance on mobile and desktop.",
    "Accessible images, charts, captions, transcripts, and downloadable assets.",
    "Canonical URLs and clean indexation rules for campaign pages and event pages."
  ]}
/>

Keep the information architecture simple. Many space sites bury important material in PDFs or event microsites, which makes indexing and user journeys harder. If a page matters to the public, put the full, discoverable version on the web page itself and use the PDF as a supporting asset rather than the primary source.

## SEO for AI search

AI search has changed how people discover information, but it has not replaced SEO; it has raised the bar. To appear well in AI summaries and answer engines, your site needs explicit terminology, trustworthy authorship, and content that states facts without unnecessary jargon. That is especially important for space topics where precision matters.

For space organisations, this means writing with named missions, instruments, agencies, dates, and technical terms instead of vague branding language. It also means adding context that helps models and users understand why the page matters. The content should answer questions like:

- What is this mission?
- Who is it for?
- What does the data do?
- Why does it matter?

within the first few paragraphs.

## Keyword clusters

Target clusters that reflect real user intent:

- Space organisation SEO
- Earth observation content strategy
- Satellite communications marketing
- Astronomy outreach resources
- Space policy communications
- Climate and space applications
- Mission updates and data portals
- Space sector careers
- Research communication for space

## Conclusion

The organisations that win in 2026 are not the ones publishing the most content. They are the ones publishing the right content, with a clear information architecture, strong internal linking, and enough technical quality for both search engines and human readers. For space brands, SEO now sits at the intersection of communications, education, accessibility, and digital infrastructure.
How to go outside and start observing the night sky with confidence, using nothing but your eyes, a little preparation and a few simple habits.

<!-- Route: /resources/stargazing/beginners-guide/ (add a matching route or move to /journal/ until then) -->

You do not need a telescope, dark-sky trip or detailed knowledge of constellations to begin stargazing. Start with your eyes, a safe outdoor location and a little time to let the sky become familiar.

That last part matters most. The night sky rewards patience more than equipment. After twenty minutes outside, your eyes will show you far more than they did when you stepped through the door: fainter stars, the texture of the Moon, the slow drift of a satellite, perhaps the smudge of a cluster. This guide takes you from "I don't know where to look" to a first confident evening under the sky, and gives you a short list of things worth finding.

## What you need

Stargazing is one of the cheapest hobbies there is. The essentials are mostly about comfort and safety.

- **Warm clothing.** You will be standing or sitting still, so you will feel colder than you expect, even on a mild evening. Add layers, a hat, gloves and warm footwear. Hot drinks help.
- **A safe place with an unobstructed view.** More on this below.
- **A red light.** Your eyes take time to adapt to darkness, and white light undoes that in seconds. A torch with a red filter or a red-light setting preserves your night vision. A bicycle rear light also works in a pinch.
- **A chair or blanket.** Looking up for long periods strains your neck. A reclining garden chair or a mat to lie on makes the evening far more enjoyable.
- **Optional: a phone, planisphere or binoculars.** A sky-map app or a planisphere helps you identify what you are seeing. Ordinary binoculars reveal craters on the Moon, the moons of Jupiter and many star clusters, but you can leave them at home for your first few sessions.

## Choose your location

The best place is the one you will actually use. A dark, remote site is ideal, but a garden or local park is a perfectly good place to start.

- **Garden, park or local dark-sky site.** Begin close to home. Once you know what you are looking at, a trip to a darker site will feel like a reward rather than a necessity. Look for designated dark-sky sites if you want a more dramatic view. [source: Dark Sky Discovery / International Dark-Sky Association]
- **Horizon visibility.** Trees, buildings and hills can hide large parts of the sky. Planets and the Moon spend much of their time low down, so a view towards the south (in the UK) and towards the east and west horizons is especially useful.
- **Light pollution.** Artificial light scatters in the atmosphere and washes out faint objects. Moving away from street lights, floodlights and car parks, or simply putting a wall or hedge between you and a bright light, makes a real difference. See the box below.
- **Personal safety.** Tell someone where you are going, take a charged phone, and avoid unlit roads, cliffs, water margins and places you would not feel comfortable at night. Do not trespass on private land, and keep to public footpaths and open access land. If you are going to a remote site, go with a friend.
- **Weather and cloud.** Check the forecast before heading out, especially cloud cover. Clear skies are not the whole story: haze, high thin cloud and humidity all reduce how many stars you can see. Forecasts change quickly, so check again just before you leave.

> **Light pollution in brief.** Light pollution is artificial light that brightens the night sky. In towns and cities it can hide all but the brightest stars. Sky darkness is often described using the Bortle scale, where lower numbers mean darker skies. You can still enjoy the Moon, bright planets and the brightest stars from a city, but the Milky Way generally needs a properly dark site. [source: International Dark-Sky Association; verify Bortle scale wording]

## Choose the right time

- **Astronomical darkness.** Twilight is divided into stages. Civil twilight ends when the Sun is 6 degrees below the horizon, nautical twilight when it reaches 12 degrees, and astronomical twilight when it reaches 18 degrees. Only after that is the sky as dark as it gets. In the UK, deep summer nights never reach full astronomical darkness in the Midlands and further north, so the darkest skies come in autumn, winter and spring. [source: official almanac; check local twilight times]
- **Moon phase.** A bright Moon lights up the sky and drowns out faint objects. Around new Moon is best for the Milky Way and faint clusters. The Moon is itself a superb target, and its best detail appears along the line between light and dark, called the terminator, rather than at full Moon.
- **Seasonal constellations.** What you see depends on the season, because Earth's orbit changes which part of the sky faces away from the Sun at night. Orion dominates winter evenings, while the Milky Way is easiest to spot in late summer and autumn from dark sites.
- **Twilight.** Do not skip it. Some of the best sights occur just after sunset, when Venus, Jupiter or the crescent Moon may be visible against a deep blue sky before the stars appear.
- **Cloud and transparency.** Transparency describes how clear the air is. On a night of good transparency, faint stars are easy to see. After rain, or when a cold front has passed, the air is often much clearer. Astronomers also talk about "seeing", which is how steady the air is, and matters mainly for telescopes.

## Learn the sky's basic movements

You do not need to memorise the sky, but a few ideas make it far less confusing.

- **East-to-west apparent motion.** The Sun, Moon, planets and stars all rise in the east and set in the west. This happens because Earth is spinning towards the east. The sky turns about 15 degrees each hour.
- **Seasonal changes.** Because Earth also orbits the Sun, a star rises about four minutes earlier each night. Over weeks, this shifts which constellations are visible at a given time in the evening, and over a year the whole sky cycles round.
- **Circumpolar stars.** From the UK, some stars never set. They circle the pole star, Polaris, all night long. The Plough and Cassiopeia are the best-known examples, which makes them useful anchors that you can find in any season.
- **The ecliptic.** The Sun, Moon and planets all follow roughly the same path across the sky, called the ecliptic. If you spot a bright, steady "star" that is not twinkling much and is close to this path, it may well be a planet. Almanacs and apps will tell you which.
- **Why the sky differs with latitude.** The stars you can see depend on how far north or south you are. Polaris sits at an altitude roughly equal to your latitude, so it is quite high in the UK sky. Further south you see stars that never rise for us, such as the Southern Cross. At the equator you can see nearly the whole sky over a year. In the southern hemisphere, familiar constellations such as Orion appear upside down compared with the UK.

**A handy measuring tool.** At arm's length, your little finger covers about 1 degree of sky, your closed fist about 10 degrees, and your outstretched hand (thumb to little finger) about 20 degrees. Many star charts describe distances this way. [source: verify with a planetarium tool]

## Start with bright targets

Begin with things that are easy to find. Confidence grows quickly when you succeed.

- **The Moon.** The easiest and most rewarding first target. Look for dark plains, bright highlands and, with binoculars, craters. When the Moon is a thin crescent you may also see earthshine, the faint glow on the unlit part.
- **Bright planets.** Venus is usually the brightest object after the Moon, seen low in the west after sunset or in the east before sunrise. Jupiter and Saturn are also easy to find when they are well placed, and Mars appears as a steady reddish point. Which planets are visible changes through the year, so check an almanac or app for the date. [source: official almanac; do not hard-code planet positions]
- **Orion.** In winter evenings, look south for three stars in a short line forming Orion's Belt. Above and to the left is red-orange Betelgeuse, below and to the right is blue-white Rigel. Below the belt, a fuzzy patch in the "sword" is the Orion Nebula, a star-forming region visible to the naked eye under dark skies. Follow the line of the belt down and to the left to find Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.
- **The Plough (Big Dipper).** Seven bright stars forming a saucepan shape. The two stars at the end of the "pan" point to Polaris. The distance from the pointers to Polaris is roughly five times the gap between the pointers themselves.
- **Cassiopeia.** A distinctive "W" or "M" shape on the opposite side of Polaris from the Plough. It is high in the sky on autumn evenings.
- **The Pleiades.** A small, tight cluster of stars in Taurus, often called the Seven Sisters. Most people see six or so with the naked eye, and binoculars reveal many more. Look for it on autumn and winter evenings.
- **The Milky Way, from a darker location.** From a properly dark site, our own galaxy appears as a pale band arching across the sky. It is easiest to see on moonless nights in late summer and autumn.

## Use a sky map

A sky map turns a confusing scatter of stars into a set of names and patterns.

- **Interactive map.** Free tools such as Stellarium (desktop and web) let you set your location and time, then show what is above you. They are good for planning and for identifying an unfamiliar bright object. [source: Stellarium project]
- **Planisphere.** A rotating card chart set to your latitude. It needs no battery, does not ruin your night vision and shows you how the sky changes with date and time. Buy one made for the latitude of the UK.
- **Mobile app.** Point-and-identify apps are convenient. Turn the brightness down and use night mode so the screen does not spoil your dark adaptation.
- **Confirm the date, time and location.** Most confusion comes from a map set to the wrong time or place. Check all three before you conclude that something is missing.
- **Treat app predictions cautiously.** Apps and websites can overstate how bright or visible something will be. Cloud, haze, light pollution and low altitude all make objects fainter than the display suggests. Use them as a guide, not a promise.

## Keep an observing log

A log turns a pleasant evening into a skill. It does not need to be elaborate: a notebook or a notes app will do. Record:

- **Date and time.** Include the time zone, or use UTC.
- **Location.** A place name or a rough grid reference is enough.
- **Weather.** Cloud cover, temperature and how clear the air felt.
- **Moon phase.** It explains a lot about what you could and could not see.
- **Equipment.** Naked eye, binoculars (note the type), or a telescope.
- **What you saw.** Objects found, first impressions, anything surprising.
- **Sketches or photographs.** A rough sketch forces you to look closely and is worth more than it seems. Phone photographs of the Moon or bright planets are a good starting point.

After a few weeks you will notice patterns: how long it takes your eyes to adapt, which conditions are best, and how the sky changes.

## Safety

- **Never look at the Sun through binoculars or a telescope without a properly designed solar filter.** Even a brief glance through unfiltered optics can cause permanent eye damage. Filters must fit securely over the front of the instrument. Ordinary sunglasses are not safe. For solar eclipse viewing by eye, use glasses that meet the relevant safety standard. [source: Royal Astronomical Society / official eclipse safety guidance; verify standard]
- **Protect dark adaptation.** Keep white light to a minimum. Use a red torch, dim your phone, and warn friends before switching on a bright light. It can take 20 to 30 minutes to reach good dark adaptation, and it is lost in moments. [source: verify adaptation time]
- **Avoid unsafe locations.** Do not stargaze on roadsides, near cliff edges, on frozen water or in places where you would be alone and vulnerable.
- **Check local conditions before travelling.** Look at the weather, road conditions and any access restrictions. In cold weather, wear more than you think you need and take a hot drink.
- **Be a considerate neighbour.** Avoid shining lights at houses and take care not to disturb wildlife or livestock.

You do not need a telescope, dark-sky trip or detailed knowledge of constellations to begin stargazing. Start with your eyes, a safe outdoor location and a little time to let the sky become familiar.

That last part matters most. The night sky rewards patience more than equipment. After twenty minutes outside, your eyes will show you far more than they did when you stepped through the door: fainter stars, the texture of the Moon, the slow drift of a satellite, perhaps the smudge of a cluster. This guide takes you from “I don’t know where to look” to a first confident evening under the sky, and gives you a short list of things worth finding.

What you need

Stargazing is one of the cheapest hobbies there is. The essentials are mostly about comfort and safety.

  • Warm clothing. You will be standing or sitting still, so you will feel colder than you expect, even on a mild evening. Add layers, a hat, gloves and warm footwear. Hot drinks help.
  • A safe place with an unobstructed view. More on this below.
  • A red light. Your eyes take time to adapt to darkness, and white light undoes that in seconds. A torch with a red filter or a red-light setting preserves your night vision. A bicycle rear light also works in a pinch.
  • A chair or blanket. Looking up for long periods strains your neck. A reclining garden chair or a mat to lie on makes the evening far more enjoyable.
  • Optional: a phone, planisphere or binoculars. A sky-map app or a planisphere helps you identify what you are seeing. Ordinary binoculars reveal craters on the Moon, the moons of Jupiter and many star clusters, but you can leave them at home for your first few sessions.

Choose your location

The best place is the one you will actually use. A dark, remote site is ideal, but a garden or local park is a perfectly good place to start.

  • Garden, park or local dark-sky site. Begin close to home. Once you know what you are looking at, a trip to a darker site will feel like a reward rather than a necessity. Look for designated dark-sky sites if you want a more dramatic view. [source: Dark Sky Discovery / International Dark-Sky Association]
  • Horizon visibility. Trees, buildings and hills can hide large parts of the sky. Planets and the Moon spend much of their time low down, so a view towards the south (in the UK) and towards the east and west horizons is especially useful.
  • Light pollution. Artificial light scatters in the atmosphere and washes out faint objects. Moving away from street lights, floodlights and car parks, or simply putting a wall or hedge between you and a bright light, makes a real difference. See the box below.
  • Personal safety. Tell someone where you are going, take a charged phone, and avoid unlit roads, cliffs, water margins and places you would not feel comfortable at night. Do not trespass on private land, and keep to public footpaths and open access land. If you are going to a remote site, go with a friend.
  • Weather and cloud. Check the forecast before heading out, especially cloud cover. Clear skies are not the whole story: haze, high thin cloud and humidity all reduce how many stars you can see. Forecasts change quickly, so check again just before you leave.

Light pollution in brief. Light pollution is artificial light that brightens the night sky. In towns and cities it can hide all but the brightest stars. Sky darkness is often described using the Bortle scale, where lower numbers mean darker skies. You can still enjoy the Moon, bright planets and the brightest stars from a city, but the Milky Way generally needs a properly dark site. [source: International Dark-Sky Association; verify Bortle scale wording]

Choose the right time

  • Astronomical darkness. Twilight is divided into stages. Civil twilight ends when the Sun is 6 degrees below the horizon, nautical twilight when it reaches 12 degrees, and astronomical twilight when it reaches 18 degrees. Only after that is the sky as dark as it gets. In the UK, deep summer nights never reach full astronomical darkness in the Midlands and further north, so the darkest skies come in autumn, winter and spring. [source: official almanac; check local twilight times]
  • Moon phase. A bright Moon lights up the sky and drowns out faint objects. Around new Moon is best for the Milky Way and faint clusters. The Moon is itself a superb target, and its best detail appears along the line between light and dark, called the terminator, rather than at full Moon.
  • Seasonal constellations. What you see depends on the season, because Earth’s orbit changes which part of the sky faces away from the Sun at night. Orion dominates winter evenings, while the Milky Way is easiest to spot in late summer and autumn from dark sites.
  • Twilight. Do not skip it. Some of the best sights occur just after sunset, when Venus, Jupiter or the crescent Moon may be visible against a deep blue sky before the stars appear.
  • Cloud and transparency. Transparency describes how clear the air is. On a night of good transparency, faint stars are easy to see. After rain, or when a cold front has passed, the air is often much clearer. Astronomers also talk about “seeing”, which is how steady the air is, and matters mainly for telescopes.

Learn the sky’s basic movements

You do not need to memorise the sky, but a few ideas make it far less confusing.

  • East-to-west apparent motion. The Sun, Moon, planets and stars all rise in the east and set in the west. This happens because Earth is spinning towards the east. The sky turns about 15 degrees each hour.
  • Seasonal changes. Because Earth also orbits the Sun, a star rises about four minutes earlier each night. Over weeks, this shifts which constellations are visible at a given time in the evening, and over a year the whole sky cycles round.
  • Circumpolar stars. From the UK, some stars never set. They circle the pole star, Polaris, all night long. The Plough and Cassiopeia are the best-known examples, which makes them useful anchors that you can find in any season.
  • The ecliptic. The Sun, Moon and planets all follow roughly the same path across the sky, called the ecliptic. If you spot a bright, steady “star” that is not twinkling much and is close to this path, it may well be a planet. Almanacs and apps will tell you which.
  • Why the sky differs with latitude. The stars you can see depend on how far north or south you are. Polaris sits at an altitude roughly equal to your latitude, so it is quite high in the UK sky. Further south you see stars that never rise for us, such as the Southern Cross. At the equator you can see nearly the whole sky over a year. In the southern hemisphere, familiar constellations such as Orion appear upside down compared with the UK.

A handy measuring tool. At arm’s length, your little finger covers about 1 degree of sky, your closed fist about 10 degrees, and your outstretched hand (thumb to little finger) about 20 degrees. Many star charts describe distances this way. [source: verify with a planetarium tool]

This year was also the 25th anniversary of the founding of UKSEDS, and we had a ‘Birthday Social’ aboard the boat ‘Under the Stars’ in Bristol Harbour!

In 2014, the National Student Space Conference was hosted by Leicester AstRoSoc at the University of Leicester. The conference was attended by industry experts such as the ESA astronaut Major Tim Peake. Our keynote speakers were Dr David Parker, the UK Space Agency Chief Executive, and Professor Richard Brown, Director of the Centre for Future Air-Space Transportation Technology at the University of Strathclyde in Glasgow. The sponsors for the event included Telespazio, Reaction Engines and the UK Space Agency.

On 1st and 2nd March, space enthusiasts descended on the University of Leicester for the UKSEDS National Student Space Conference 2014. Aimed at UK students, each year the conference is a key opportunity to meet and network with a wide range of people in the space sector from academia to industry, across multiple disciplines. It is also a great time for students from UKSEDS’ various branches to meet together in one place and discuss their activities. This year the event was in its 26th year.

The conference was a real sell-out once again with over 250 delegates* from many UKSEDS branches spanning the width and breadth of the country — from Edinburgh to Kent to Southampton, Exeter, Manchester and Strathclyde. We were also happy to welcome our international friends at SEDS-USA and EUROAVIA once again. We had a great range of talks throughout the weekend from spaceplanes to cubesats, ISS, outreach and education, space biomedicine, astronomy, Mars and beyond.

Highlights included a talk by British ESA Astronaut Major Tim Peake who Skyped in from Houston to talk about his mission alongside the outreach components of his mission, along with Jeremy Curtis (Head of Education and Outreach, UK Space Agency). There was a good chance of a Q&A and for delegates to engage with Tim. He revealed how his mission is being prepared and how his food and drinks will be sent up in advance, sharing his love of Yorkshire Tea. Sheffield SEDS (ShefSEDS) tweeted this, amusingly re-tweeted and replied to by Yorkshire Tea:


Our Saturday keynote included Prof. Richard Brown from the Centre for Future Air-Space Transportation Technology, University of Strathclyde who gave a very inspiring talk on ‘Shock Waves and the Design of Future Spacecraft’.

Following this, delegates were invited to a networking reception, kindly sponsored by Reaction Engines Ltd. After which, delegates could attend the UKSEDS social and enjoy a tasty buffet meal and mingle with other delegates.

Sunday morning started with Dr David Parker (CEO, UK Space Agency) who spoke about the latest developments on UK Space activities.

Throughout the weekend Telespazio Vega Deutschland demonstrated their Satellite Operations Training simulator, allowing delegates to simulate real in-orbit satellite operations throughout the conference.

Cover for Ecosend podcast episode S4E10: Sustainability and Space?!

The EcoSend Podcast explores how to build a truly climate-conscious business, covering sustainability, marketing, startups, software, and space. This episode continues that mission with a focused conversation about space sustainability and satellite technology.
An episode about sustainability and space, including satellite data, space debris, and climate impact.

## Episode overview

When it comes to sustainability, we usually think about life here on Earth. This episode asks what happens when we extend that conversation into space.

James Gill speaks with Ryan Laird, Founder and Director of Green Orbit Digital, about how satellite data and space technology can support climate action and better environmental decision-making.

## Topics covered

- Ryan’s journey from Physics to Marketing and Space Sustainability.
- The rise of private ventures in the space industry.
- The challenge of integrating sustainable practice into satellite management.
- How satellite data can help safeguard the future against climate change.
- The idea of creating a digital twin of the world to monitor planetary health and inform environmental policy.

## Key takeaway

The episode argues that sustainability should apply not only to our work on Earth, but also to how we build, launch, and manage technology in space.

## About Ryan Laird

Ryan Laird is the Founder and Director of Green Orbit Digital, where he helps businesses navigate the intersection of digital marketing and sustainability in the space industry.

Models of Time-dependent Accretion Discs with Outflows

Numerical investigation of time-dependent accretion-disc evolution with mass feedback and outflows. The project developed and validated a Fortran model based on Shakura-Sunyaev disc solutions and wind-infall formulations to examine disc dynamics, angular-momentum transport and wind energy deposition.
R. J. M. Laird / University of Leicester
Numerical plot of temperature, pressure and radial properties in steady-state and time-dependent accretion-disc models with wind feedback.

Developed and tested a numerical model for time-dependent accretion discs supplied by wind-fed material. The simulations indicated that large-scale wind deposition can dominate disc evolution across extreme angular-momentum assumptions, while small-scale deposition produces more distinct mass-retention and depletion behaviour.
Validated steady-state alpha-disc solutions against gas- and radiation-pressure regimes
Implemented time-dependent surface-density diffusion and mass-conservation calculations
Verified viscous spreading using Gaussian-ring test conditions
Simulated large-scale and small-scale wind-feedback regimes
Compared extreme angular-momentum cases for supplied material
Completed final-year undergraduate research under Dr Sergei Nayakshin

## Overview

Accretion discs are rotating structures of gas that form when material falls
towards a compact object while retaining angular momentum. They are found around
young stars, white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes, including the
supermassive black holes that power active galactic nuclei (AGN).

For gas to move inward and accrete, angular momentum must be transported
outwards through the disc. The widely used Shakura-Sunyaev alpha-disc model
represents this transport through an effective viscosity parameter, alpha. The
model provides a useful framework for describing thin, radiatively efficient
accretion discs. [web:190][web:194]

This final-year undergraduate research project developed a numerical model of
an accretion disc evolving over time while receiving matter and energy from
stellar winds or other external mass inflow. The work investigated how the
spatial scale and angular momentum of supplied material influence disc
structure, mass loss and black-hole feeding.

## Research question

How do mass outflows, wind feedback and the angular momentum of supplied
material affect the long-term evolution of a time-dependent accretion disc?

The project addressed several connected questions:

- Can a numerical steady-state disc model reproduce established analytical
  solutions?
- Can the resulting code accurately evolve surface density through viscous
  diffusion while conserving total mass?
- Does a wind deposited over a large radial scale alter disc evolution
  differently from a wind concentrated near the central object?
- How sensitive are disc depletion and accretion behaviour to the angular
  momentum carried by injected material?
- What insight can idealised wind-fed discs provide for low-luminosity galactic
  nuclei such as Sagittarius A*?

## Theoretical context

### Accretion and angular momentum

Gas with substantial angular momentum typically settles into a disc rather than
falling directly towards a compact object. It can only move inward if angular
momentum is redistributed, generally through viscous or turbulent stresses.

In the standard alpha-disc prescription, kinematic viscosity is represented by:

\[
\nu = \alpha c_{\mathrm{s}} H
\]

where \(\nu\) is the kinematic viscosity, \(\alpha\) is a dimensionless
efficiency parameter, \(c_{\mathrm{s}}\) is the sound speed and \(H\) is the
disc scale height. [web:194][web:197]

### Shakura-Sunyaev discs

The project used Shakura-Sunyaev thin-disc solutions as the initial and
validation framework. In this approach, disc properties depend on the central
mass, mass-accretion rate, viscosity parameter and radial distance from the
accretor. The model includes regimes in which gas pressure or radiation pressure
dominates the disc structure. [web:195][web:196]

### Wind-fed accretion

The model then extended the steady-state framework to consider time-dependent
mass injection and wind feedback. External material can alter a disc's surface
density, angular-momentum balance and accretion rate, particularly when the
incoming material has a different angular momentum from gas already orbiting in
the disc.

The project used modified conservation equations based on wind-infall
formulations associated with Falcke, Melia and collaborators. These models
provide a simplified way to explore the interaction between wind-fed material,
disc evolution and accretion onto a central black hole. [web:191]

## Numerical model

The numerical model was implemented in **Fortran 77**, with output analysis and
visualisation performed in **IDL**.

The simulation considered a central black hole with an assumed mass of:

```text
10^8 solar masses
```

The baseline calculations used:

```text
Accretion rate: 0.1 times the Eddington accretion rate
Viscosity parameter: alpha = 0.1
```

The Eddington limit provides a reference scale at which radiation pressure from
accretion luminosity can oppose further spherical inflow. In realistic disc
systems, the relationship between supplied mass, radiation, outflows and
accretion can be more complex than this idealised reference value.

## Method

### Steady-state validation

The initial stage of the project implemented a steady-state disc solver.

Disc profiles were calculated over a range of radii and compared with
analytical solutions associated with Svensson and Zdziarski. The validation
tested the expected transition between gas-pressure-dominated and
radiation-pressure-dominated regimes.

This stage established that the numerical implementation reproduced the
qualitative behaviour expected of standard thin-disc models before
time-dependent terms were introduced.

### Time-dependent diffusion

The model was then extended to evolve the surface-density distribution,
\(\Sigma(r,t)\), over time.

The numerical solution treated viscous evolution as a radial diffusion process.
At each time step, the program updated the mass distribution across the disc
while tracking total system mass.

Mass-conservation testing showed that the implementation maintained a stable
total mass of approximately:

```text
100,729.7 solar masses
```

within the numerical precision and boundary assumptions of the model.

### Gaussian-ring tests

A Gaussian ring of material was used as a controlled test case for the
time-dependent solver.

Under viscous evolution, an initially narrow ring should spread radially:
some material moves inwards and can accrete, while some transports angular
momentum outwards. The numerical code reproduced this expected spreading
behaviour and approached stationary constant-accretion-rate solutions under
the relevant boundary conditions.

### Wind-feedback implementation

The final stage introduced source terms representing wind-fed mass and energy
deposition.

The calculations compared two idealised regimes:

- **Large-scale wind deposition**, in which material was supplied over an
  extended radial region, with a collection area reaching approximately
  0.1 parsecs.
- **Small-scale wind deposition**, in which supplied material was concentrated
  more closely around the disc.

The simulations also tested extreme angular-momentum conditions for the
incoming material:

- \(\xi = 1\), representing supplied matter with high or maximum assumed
  angular momentum.
- \(\xi = 0\), representing supplied matter with negligible assumed angular
  momentum.

These cases were not intended as complete physical models of all wind-fed
systems. They were controlled experiments for identifying which assumptions
had the strongest influence on the disc's evolution.

## Findings

### Large-scale wind deposition

In the large-scale wind models, wind supply dominated the evolution of the
disc.

The simulations showed little difference between the extreme angular-momentum
cases, \(\xi = 1\) and \(\xi = 0\). Once material was deposited over a broad
enough radial region, the large-scale mass and energy input determined the
overall disc evolution more strongly than the angular momentum parameter of
the injected material.

This result suggested that, in this idealised regime, the spatial distribution
of wind deposition is more important than the angular-momentum contrast between
the two tested cases.

### Small-scale wind deposition

Small-scale wind models displayed more distinct depletion behaviour.

The disc mass declined more gradually at first than in the large-scale cases,
then underwent a sharper reduction after approximately one million years in
the low-angular-momentum condition.

The models also indicated lower final black-hole mass growth than the
large-scale cases, by roughly 10 percent under the assumptions used in the
simulation.

### Super-Eddington phases

Across the tested parameter space, the calculated accretion rates remained
above the reference Eddington rate for extended periods, broadly from
\(10^5\) to \(10^6\) years, before declining as the available disc material was
depleted.

These phases should be interpreted within the model's idealised assumptions.
A complete treatment of super-Eddington accretion would require more detailed
radiative transfer, geometry, outflow launching and magnetohydrodynamics than
were included here.

### Relevance to galactic nuclei

The calculations provided a simplified framework for considering wind-fed
accretion near supermassive black holes, including environments such as the
Galactic Centre.

Such systems can receive substantial mass input from nearby stars while
remaining relatively faint in radiative output. The project illustrated how
the location, angular momentum and feedback associated with supplied wind
material can affect the rate at which gas reaches the central black hole.

## Contribution

I completed this project independently as a final-year undergraduate physics
student at the University of Leicester under the supervision of **Dr Sergei
Nayakshin**.

My work included:

- Implementing core steady-state disc calculations in Fortran 77.
- Building a time-dependent surface-density diffusion solver.
- Testing mass conservation and numerical stability.
- Performing Gaussian-ring validation experiments.
- Adding parameterised wind-feedback and mass-injection terms.
- Producing IDL routines for diagnostic plots and model comparison.
- Writing the final project dissertation.

## Related output

### Models of Time-dependent Accretion Discs with Outflows

**R. J. M. Laird**

Undergraduate Final Year Project Report, Department of Physics and Astronomy,
University of Leicester, 27 February 2009.

Supervised by Dr Sergei Nayakshin.

The dissertation documented the theoretical framework, numerical algorithms,
Fortran implementation, stability and conservation tests, and comparative
evolution plots for wind-fed accretion-disc models.

## Scientific significance

Accretion discs connect small-scale gas physics with some of the most luminous
phenomena in the Universe. Their behaviour affects black-hole growth, stellar
evolution, jet production, AGN activity and the feedback between compact
objects and their surroundings.

This project examined a focused aspect of that problem: how external wind
supply changes a disc over time. It showed, within the model assumptions, that
the radial scale of wind deposition can dominate the outcome, while the
angular-momentum state of incoming material becomes more influential when
deposition is confined to a smaller region.

## Limitations

This was an idealised one-dimensional numerical model, with several important
limitations:

- It used a parameterised alpha-viscosity prescription rather than resolving
  magnetohydrodynamic turbulence.
- It did not model three-dimensional disc structure, warping or non-axisymmetric
  instabilities.
- Wind mass, energy and angular momentum were introduced through simplified
  source terms rather than self-consistent wind-launching calculations.
- Radiative transfer and radiation-pressure feedback were treated through
  simplified disc assumptions.
- Magnetic fields, jet launching and detailed outflow geometry were not included.
- Results depended on the adopted central mass, viscosity, initial conditions,
  deposition profile and boundary conditions.

The results therefore provide insight into the behaviour of the model rather
than a complete prediction for any specific accreting black-hole system.

  • Results depended on the adopted central mass, viscosity, initial conditions, deposition profile and boundary conditions.

The results therefore provide insight into the behaviour of the model rather than a complete prediction for any specific accreting black-hole system.

## Overview

**Securing Aeolus Against Atomic Oxygen** is a short European Space Agency
documentary about a small but important spacecraft-engineering problem:
protecting satellite materials from atomic oxygen in low Earth orbit.

The film follows testing undertaken for ESA’s **Aeolus** wind-mapping mission.
It shows how engineers at ESA’s Materials and Electrical Components Laboratory
assessed the resilience of protective beta cloth, using an atomic-oxygen
generator followed by microscopic inspection. [web:283]

I contributed script development through Design & Data, helping make a
specialist materials-science process understandable to a public audience.

## The challenge

At ground level, oxygen normally exists as stable molecules,
\(\mathrm{O_2}\). At the upper edge of Earth’s atmosphere, ultraviolet
radiation can split those molecules into individual oxygen atoms.

This **atomic oxygen** is highly reactive. Spacecraft operating in low Earth
orbit move through it at orbital speed, exposing surfaces to an environment
capable of eroding, oxidising or changing the properties of some materials.
[web:280][web:287]

The communications challenge was to make an invisible environmental risk
visible:
→ Sunlight breaks oxygen molecules apart
→ Atomic oxygen forms at high altitude
→ Satellites encounter it at orbital speed
→ Vulnerable materials can erode
→ Testing informs spacecraft design

## Atomic oxygen in orbit

Atomic oxygen is a major component of the low Earth orbit environment at
altitudes where the residual atmosphere is still present.

Spacecraft motion through this environment produces energetic impacts on
exposed surfaces. Organic materials, coatings and some polymers can be
especially susceptible to erosion or changes in surface properties. [web:287]

The phenomenon became widely recognised after early Space Shuttle flights
returned with visible degradation to thermal-blanket materials. ESA’s video
uses this history to explain why spacecraft designers must account for the
atomic-oxygen environment before launch. [web:283]

## Aeolus mission context

Aeolus was ESA’s Earth-observation mission for measuring global wind profiles.
Its instrument used lidar technology to observe winds in the atmosphere,
supporting improved understanding of weather, climate and atmospheric
dynamics.

The satellite was designed for low Earth orbit, where components and exposed
materials had to withstand the local space environment throughout the mission.

Aeolus ended operations in April 2023, but the engineering lessons associated
with its development remain relevant to later Earth-observation and low-orbit
missions. [web:286]

## Beta-cloth testing

The documentary focused on **beta cloth**, a protective fibre material intended
for use on Aeolus.

ESA’s Materials and Electrical Components Laboratory tested the material using
an atomic-oxygen generator. This allowed the engineering team to expose
candidate material to a simulated version of the orbital environment before
the spacecraft was launched. [web:283]

After exposure, the material was inspected under a microscope to identify
evidence of surface damage or degradation.

The test sequence can be summarised as:
→ Candidate material
→ Simulated atomic-oxygen exposure
→ Microscopic inspection
→ Assessment of material resilience
→ More reliable spacecraft design

## Laboratory simulation

Ground testing is essential because spacecraft designers cannot wait for a
mission to fly before discovering whether its materials can survive the space
environment.

ESA’s Low Earth Orbit Facility generates atomic oxygen in a vacuum chamber to
reproduce the energy associated with orbital exposure. The facility can produce
an atomic-oxygen beam with energies equivalent to spacecraft travelling at
approximately 7.8 km/s. [web:289]

Such facilities enable engineers to test candidate materials under controlled
conditions, compare their performance and select protective approaches suitable
for the intended orbit and mission duration.

## My role

I worked as a **Scriptwriter** through Design & Data.

My contribution included:

- Developing the documentary narrative and script structure.
- Translating atomic-oxygen physics into accessible language.
- Explaining the relationship between space environment, material testing and
  mission reliability.
- Supporting the communication of laboratory processes and technical visuals.
- Connecting a small-scale materials experiment with the large-scale purpose of
  an Earth-observation mission.

The objective was to retain scientific and engineering accuracy while providing
a story that could be followed by viewers without a background in materials
science or spacecraft design.

## Editorial approach

The film used a contrast between familiar oxygen on Earth and the reactive
atomic oxygen found near the edge of space.

The oxygen we breathe
is not the oxygen a low-orbiting satellite encounters.

This gave the documentary an accessible opening before moving into the
specialised work of laboratory testing, protective materials and spacecraft
qualification.

Rather than presenting materials science as an abstract engineering discipline,
the narrative framed it as a practical safeguard: testing what can happen to a
material before it becomes part of an operational satellite.

## Outcome

The completed documentary was released by ESA in June 2016.

ESA lists **Securing Aeolus against atomic oxygen** as a four-minute,
English-language documentary released on 24 June 2016. The official description
identifies beta-cloth testing, atomic-oxygen generation and microscopic
inspection as the central elements of the story. [web:283][web:285]

## Limitations

This project concerned science communication and documentary scripting. It did

The test described in the film examined a specific material under controlled

AMBIEnT was an International Space University team project designing a low-cost microsatellite constellation to bring internet access, tele-education, telemedicine and community environmental monitoring to the unconnected Brazilian Amazon, with the potential to expand to other remote regions.
A sun conure parrot flying above a satellite view of South America with the Brazilian Amazon highlighted, the AMBIEnT mission visual.
