## Overview

AMBIEnT (Affordable Microsatellite-Based Internet Access and Environmental
Monitoring) was a conceptual design study completed as part of the
International Space University (ISU) Space Studies Program 2013 in Strasbourg.
The challenge was tackled by 33 participants from 19 countries.

The mission statement was to offer **sustainable and affordable internet access
and environmental monitoring via a constellation of microsatellites by 2018**,
as a means to provide socio-economic benefits to the Brazilian Amazon region,
with a future capability for global expansion to other remote areas.

The team was chaired by Marco Chamon (INPE) with co-chair Walter Abrahão,
teaching associate Raycho Raychev and emerging chair Dag Evensberget.

## The challenge

Around 26 million people in the Brazilian Amazon were without reliable
internet access. Terrestrial networks struggle in a region of dense forest,
long distances and limited infrastructure, widening the digital divide with the
rest of the country.

AMBIEnT had to address several linked problems at once:

- Providing basic connectivity at a cost communities could actually sustain.
- Delivering practical services, not only bandwidth: education and healthcare.
- Giving communities tools to help detect and report illegal deforestation.
- Keeping programme costs low enough to be realistic for a microsatellite
  operator and its partners.
- Meeting international space debris mitigation guidelines.

## System concept

The architecture was split into three segments, linked through a ground
gateway to the wider internet.

### Space segment

- A constellation of 100 kg microsatellites in a 600 km equatorial orbit
  (0° inclination), giving continuous coverage over the target region.
- Based on the SSTL-100 platform, a bus designed for a seven-year lifetime and
  with a strong flight heritage.
- X-Band communications using helical antennas.
- Compact spacecraft of roughly 0.4 × 0.4 × 0.7 m, suitable for low-cost
  piggyback launches.

### Ground segment

- Two internet gateway control stations (West and East) with 3 m receiving
  antennas and signal distribution systems.
- A network of ground stations with helical antennas acting as community hubs.
- Sensor drones attached to ground stations, relaying environmental data to
  the AMBIEnT processing centre.

### User segment

- Municipalities hosting tele-education centres in schools and libraries.
- Public internet terminals in each participating municipality.
- Telemedicine terminals with health-sensor packages linking patients to
  doctors elsewhere in Brazil.
- Environmental sensors, smartphones and computers connecting to local hubs.

> **Note on figures:** the October 2013 poster describes a design of 14
> satellites, 1,161 ground stations and 129 municipalities at an estimated
> programme cost of $263M. The February 2014 presentation describes an updated
> baseline of 12 satellites, 110 ground stations, about 48,000 households
> served, 6–7 years of operational time and a total cost of about $260M over
> 10 years. The design evolved between the two presentations.

## Services

### Tele-education

Partnerships with municipalities would establish tele-education centres in
schools and libraries, supported by technical education so that local people
could operate and maintain the equipment.

### Telemedicine

Two options were considered:

- **Partnership model:** AMBIEnT supplies connectivity and existing telehealth
  services provide the medical service.
- **Own platform:** a laptop with text and voice capabilities, a simple user
  interface and a health-sensor package.

### Environmental monitoring

Fixed and mobile ground sensing, together with smartphone apps and weather
monitoring, would support timely alerts of illegal deforestation. The aim was
to empower communities to act as monitors of their own forests.

## Sustainability and business model

AMBIEnT was designed to be provided at no cost to end users. Funding was
proposed through financial support from carbon-offsetting collaboration, with
the potential for microfinance and new local markets to help sustain the
programme and reduce the digital divide.

**Implementation milestones:**

- 2015: start of production
- 2016: ground station placement begins
- 2017: first of four launches, with on-orbit testing
- 2018: constellation begins operations
- 2019–2024: continued training of key personnel

The system was planned to operate for at least seven years, with a goal of a
ten-year programme.

## Space debris mitigation

A deorbit analysis showed the satellites decaying from 600 km within about 18
years, satisfying the space debris mitigation guidelines of UN COPUOS (2010)
and the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee (IADC).

## Presentations and outputs

- **6th Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium, 7–10 October 2013:** research
  poster presented through the University of Alabama in Huntsville and the
  American Astronautical Society.
- **UN COPUOS Scientific and Technical Subcommittee, 14 February 2014:**
  presentation of the team project, delivered by Anita Rinner (ISU SSP 2013
  alumna).
- **Project video:** produced by Dawoon Jung.

## What made AMBIEnT distinctive

- An innovative low-cost solution built around microsatellites.
- A packaged offer combining telemedicine, education terminals and
  mitigation of illegal logging, rather than connectivity alone.
- A clear value proposition for communities, with the possibility of
  microfinance.
- Sustainability built into both the business model and the orbital design.

work package you led or supported, and any presentation, writing or
coordination responsibilities.

## Limitations and status

AMBIEnT was a conceptual design study and educational exercise, not a funded
flight programme. Its figures, schedules and costs were planning estimates
produced within the constraints of the ISU Space Studies Program, and would
require detailed engineering, regulatory, spectrum and financing work before
any implementation.

Bake In Space was a space-food innovation project developing a safe, low-power system for baking fresh, crumb-free bread aboard the International Space Station. The project used bread as a practical technology demonstration for improving food quality, wellbeing and long-term self-sufficiency in human spaceflight.

Supported a high-profile space-food innovation programme that developed a prototype microgravity oven and a crumb-free bread concept for the International Space Station, while communicating its relevance to astronaut wellbeing, food-system innovation and long-duration exploration.

## Overview

Bake In Space was a space-food innovation project exploring how fresh bread
could be produced safely aboard the International Space Station (ISS).

The initial objective was to bake a familiar German bread roll in microgravity.
Behind that apparently simple goal was a wider challenge: developing food
preparation technologies that could improve comfort, wellbeing and quality of
life for people living and working in space for extended periods.

The project treated bread as a practical stepping stone towards more ambitious
forms of food self-sufficiency. Future human missions beyond low Earth orbit
will require systems that use limited power, space, water and supplies
efficiently. Food production, preparation, storage, hygiene and waste
management will all be important parts of that transition.

## The challenge

Bread is difficult to prepare in space.

On Earth, bread is a familiar, low-risk food. In a spacecraft, loose crumbs can
float freely, potentially affecting ventilation systems, sensitive equipment or
crew safety. Conventional ovens also use substantial power, generate high
surface temperatures and depend on operating conditions that are unsuitable for
a tightly controlled spacecraft environment.

Bake In Space therefore had to address several connected constraints:

- Preventing crumbs from becoming a spacecraft contamination hazard.
- Limiting exterior surface temperatures to protect crew members.
- Operating within a restricted ISS power budget.
- Avoiding unsafe handling of hot air inside a pressurised spacecraft.
- Designing a suitable dough product for low-power baking.
- Ensuring food safety, hygiene and storage stability.
- Considering how the system could support future, more self-sufficient food
  production beyond Earth.

The project’s early target was a compact oven capable of baking a specially
developed dough product in microgravity while meeting applicable operational
and safety requirements.

## Why bread?

Food is more than nutrition. It supports routine, morale, comfort, cultural
identity and quality of life.

For crews spending long periods away from Earth, fresh food can provide a
meaningful improvement over a diet based mainly on pre-packaged products.
Bread was chosen not only because it is widely familiar, but because its
production brings together many of the technical challenges that future
space-food systems will need to solve.

Bake In Space positioned fresh bread as an accessible demonstration of wider
capabilities:

- Safe food preparation in microgravity.
- Low-energy cooking and processing.
- Shelf-stable or space-compatible ingredients.
- Food-quality improvements for long-duration missions.
- Technology development relevant to future lunar and Martian habitats.
- Potential terrestrial applications for resource-constrained environments.

## Technical approach

The initial Bake In Space concept centred on a compact, space-ready oven and a
dough formulation designed for microgravity.

### Low-power baking

Conventional ovens operate at high temperatures and typically require far more
electricity than could reasonably be allocated to a small ISS food experiment.
The Bake In Space oven concept was designed to operate at roughly 220–270 watts,
around one-tenth of the power used by many household ovens.

This constrained the heating process and required careful consideration of how
to produce an acceptable bread product without conventional preheating or
high-temperature baking.

### Temperature and crew safety

ISS safety requirements limited the temperature of accessible surfaces. The
oven therefore needed to avoid presenting a burn hazard to astronauts.

A proposed operating sequence involved loading the product into a cool oven,
heating through the baking cycle and then cooling before access. This differed
substantially from ordinary terrestrial baking, where bread is placed into and
removed from a hot oven.

### Crumb reduction

Crumbs are a particular challenge in microgravity because they do not settle to
the floor. Bake In Space explored dough and baking approaches intended to
produce a bread roll that remained structurally stable and reduced the risk of
loose particles.

Water management was also an important consideration. Adding moisture during
the cycle was investigated as a way to limit drying and help achieve an
appropriate texture under low-power baking conditions.

### Food safety and ingredients

The project considered the challenges of using yeast, sourdough cultures and
other biological ingredients in a spacecraft environment. Open or uncontrolled
cultures could introduce contamination risks, so ingredient stability and
hygienic handling were central to the concept.

The longer-term vision included a sequence of demonstrations spanning the
wider bread-production chain: growing grain, processing ingredients, mixing,
baking and managing waste in constrained environments.

## My role

I worked with Bake In Space as **Editor and UK Coordinator**.

My contribution focused on communicating the project’s purpose, technical
challenges and wider relevance to audiences across the space, innovation and
food sectors. This included editorial development, science communication,
project messaging and UK-facing coordination.

The role involved translating a complex engineering and food-technology concept
into clear, credible public communication. The central narrative connected a
recognisable human experience—fresh bread—with major questions about long-term
human spaceflight, sustainability and life beyond Earth.

## Communications approach

The project needed to communicate on several levels at once:

- **Technical:** explaining the constraints of baking safely in microgravity.
- **Scientific:** connecting the demonstration to research on human spaceflight
  and food systems.
- **Human:** showing why familiar, freshly prepared food matters for wellbeing.
- **Commercial:** identifying possible applications, partnerships and technology
  spin-offs.
- **Public:** making the project understandable and memorable beyond specialist
  space audiences.

The message “baking where nobody baked before” provided an accessible entry
point, while the supporting communication explained the serious engineering,
safety and sustainability work behind the concept.

## Innovation and potential applications

Bake In Space considered the ISS demonstration a first step rather than an end
in itself.

Potential long-term applications included:

- Fresh-food systems for future lunar and Mars missions.
- Compact, low-energy food-preparation technology.
- New approaches to hygienic processing in enclosed environments.
- Products and intellectual property with terrestrial applications.
- Food solutions for aircraft, ships, field environments or energy-constrained
  settings.
- Branded experiences and products connected to the commercial space sector.
- Research access to the oven platform for other ISS experiments.

The project also linked its work to the increasing commercial use of the ISS and
the broader development of human spaceflight beyond low Earth orbit.

## Recognition

Bake In Space received recognition through the **2017 INNOspace Masters**
competition. The programme highlighted the project as an example of innovation
arising from the commercialisation of the ISS and from the growing European
space-technology ecosystem.

The INNOspace Masters profile described the project’s aim of baking German
bread rolls on the ISS using a space-ready oven and dough formulation designed
for weightlessness. It also identified prospective technology and business
benefits beyond the initial demonstration. [INNOspace Masters](https://innospace-masters.de/bake-in-space/)

## Public engagement

The project attracted international interest because it made a complex
spaceflight challenge tangible.

Media coverage focused on the engineering problem of preparing a familiar food
in an unfamiliar environment: limited electrical power, strict safety limits,
the risk of crumbs and the need to develop a suitable dough product. These
stories helped connect public curiosity about space travel with the practical
work required to support human life away from Earth.

## Limitations and status

Bake In Space was an innovation and technology-demonstration programme. Its
ambition extended beyond the immediate task of baking bread in microgravity,
but many proposed future stages—such as end-to-end grain-to-bread production in
space—would require substantial further development, testing, partnership and
flight opportunities.

The project should therefore be understood as an early-stage contribution to
the broader challenge of producing fresh food safely and sustainably during
human space exploration.

## Overview

**BreezoMeter** is a global environmental-information service that provides
local, personalised information about air quality and pollen.

The service combines big-data methods and machine learning with multiple
environmental data sources, including government monitoring stations, traffic
information, meteorological conditions and data from the Copernicus Atmosphere
Monitoring Service (**CAMS**). [web:266][web:267]

This project formed part of the **European State of the Climate 2017** showcase
work for ECMWF and Copernicus. I contributed editorial and
science-communication work through Design & Data, helping explain how
large-scale atmospheric data can become clear, useful information for
individuals and organisations.

## The challenge

Air pollution and pollen are often invisible, variable and highly local.

People may know that poor air quality or high pollen levels can affect health,
comfort and daily routines, but they do not necessarily have the time or
technical knowledge to interpret pollutant concentrations, monitoring networks,
weather models or forecast uncertainty.

The communications challenge was to explain a sophisticated data pipeline in
terms of everyday questions:

- What is the air quality where I am?
- Which pollutant is likely to matter most today?
- Are pollen conditions likely to affect allergies?
- When is a better time to exercise, commute or spend time outdoors?
- How can a service provide useful information where monitoring stations are
  sparse or absent?

BreezoMeter’s public value came from making these questions easier to answer.

## The service

BreezoMeter’s aim was to provide air-quality and pollen information in a form
that users could understand as readily as a weather forecast.

The service reached both businesses and consumers through:

- A mobile application.
- An interactive website.
- Application programming interfaces (APIs).
- Data products for external platforms and organisations.

Users could explore current air-pollution and pollen conditions for a selected
location, alongside forecast information and personalised recommendations.
[web:266][web:263]

## Data approach

BreezoMeter combined several data layers to estimate local environmental
conditions:

Government monitoring stations
+ Satellite observations
+ Traffic information
+ Weather and meteorological conditions
+ CAMS atmospheric data
+ Machine learning and big-data analytics

# Food Security and Resilience Copernicus Hackathon

## Feed the World, Invent the Future

The **Food Security and Resilience Copernicus Hackathon** was a two-day collaborative innovation event held at the **University of Leicester on 19–20 September 2019**.

Bringing together coders, researchers, scientists, designers, storytellers, entrepreneurs and problem-solvers, the hackathon challenged participants to use **Copernicus Earth observation data and services** to develop practical solutions to challenges surrounding food security, water security and resilience in a changing climate.

Over an intensive **48 hours**, multidisciplinary teams developed prototypes, explored new applications for satellite data and investigated opportunities for collaboration between academia, industry and the wider community.

## About the Hackathon

The event was built around a simple challenge:

> **Feed the World, Invent the Future**

Food security requires people to have access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food while ensuring that food systems remain sustainable into the future.

Achieving this requires better understanding of the environmental, economic and societal pressures affecting food production and consumption.

The hackathon provided a practical environment in which participants could explore how Earth observation and space-enabled technologies could contribute to addressing these challenges.

## Objectives

The hackathon was designed around several interconnected objectives.

### Developing Solutions

Develop new solutions addressing local and global food and water security challenges, with a particular emphasis on resilience and sustainability.

### Raising Awareness

Increase awareness of the University of Leicester's work supporting:

- UK and European space programmes
- Environmental monitoring
- Security and resilience
- Earth observation
- Food and drink industries
- Space-enabled innovation

### Connecting Students and Industry

Give students and early-career participants the opportunity to work on real-world challenges while connecting them with businesses, researchers and wider professional networks.

### Building Collaboration

Use the Copernicus Hackathon as a mechanism for creating new collaborations between:

- Academia
- Industry
- Government
- Students
- Researchers
- Entrepreneurs
- Technology developers
- End users

## Copernicus and Earth Observation

The hackathon centred on the **Copernicus programme**, the European Union's Earth observation programme.

Copernicus provides access to extensive environmental data and services derived from satellites, in-situ observations and other sources.

Participants were encouraged to explore how this open data could be transformed into useful applications and services.

Potential applications included:

- Agriculture
- Food production
- Water security
- Environmental monitoring
- Climate resilience
- Logistics
- Supply chains
- Resource mapping
- Risk assessment
- Insurance
- Smart cities
- Decision support

The emphasis was not simply on analysing satellite data, but on turning Earth observation into practical solutions.

## Challenge Themes

Participants could select their own challenge within the broad theme of food and water security and resilience.

Suggested areas included:

### Smart Agriculture

Using Earth observation and other technologies to improve agricultural decision-making, productivity and resilience.

### Logistics and Supply Chains

Exploring how satellite data, logistics technologies and emerging digital infrastructure could improve food supply chains.

### Blockchain and Food Security

Investigating potential applications of distributed technologies in food and water supply chains, provenance and resilience.

### Smart Insurance

Developing new services that could use Earth observation data to understand environmental risks and support innovative insurance products.

### Resource Mapping

Using satellite observations to map, monitor and understand environmental and agricultural resources.

### Societal and Technical Challenges

Participants were also encouraged to identify their own challenges relevant to food security, water security and resilience.

## The 48-Hour Challenge

The core hackathon took place over **19 and 20 September 2019**.

Teams worked intensively over two days to move from an initial problem or idea towards a practical prototype.

The process encouraged rapid experimentation and multidisciplinary collaboration.

Participants combined:

- Copernicus data
- Coding
- Data analysis
- Design
- Research
- Business modelling
- Storytelling
- Domain expertise

The objective was to produce something tangible rather than simply discuss potential applications.

## Rapid MVP Development

Participants received preparatory training before the main event.

A training session on **12 September 2019** introduced selected teams and other participants to:

- Agile development
- Rapid MVP development
- Copernicus data access
- Relevant coding libraries
- Rapid prototyping approaches

This provided teams with a common foundation before the 48-hour event.

The focus on **minimum viable products (MVPs)** helped participants move rapidly from ideas towards demonstrable concepts.

## Knowledge Exchange

The hackathon was designed as a knowledge-exchange activity rather than a conventional coding competition.

It brought together people with different skills and perspectives, allowing technical expertise to be combined with knowledge of food systems, Earth observation, business and societal challenges.

This multidisciplinary approach was central to the event.

A successful solution could require expertise from several different domains, for example:

**Satellite data + agriculture + software + business + user needs**

rather than technology development in isolation.

## From Data to Impact

A central theme of the hackathon was the transformation of raw Earth observation data into useful information and ultimately actionable solutions.

The process can be represented as:

**Earth observation data → Information → Insight → Application → Impact**

Copernicus provides the data infrastructure, but the value emerges when that data is combined with domain knowledge, software, business models and an understanding of user needs.

The hackathon provided a practical environment for exploring this transition.

## Food Security and Resilience

Food security is not simply a question of producing more food.

It is influenced by a complex combination of:

- Climate
- Water availability
- Land use
- Agricultural productivity
- Supply chains
- Infrastructure
- Markets
- Environmental change
- Resource availability
- Human behaviour

Earth observation can provide a powerful perspective because satellites can repeatedly observe large areas of the planet.

This creates opportunities to monitor change, identify risks and support decisions across different scales.

## Space-Enabled Innovation

The hackathon demonstrated the potential of space technologies to contribute to challenges far beyond the traditional space sector.

Satellite data can support applications across:

- Agriculture
- Food systems
- Environmental management
- Climate adaptation
- Urban planning
- Logistics
- Insurance
- Emergency response
- Sustainability

The event therefore positioned Copernicus not simply as a source of scientific data, but as an enabling infrastructure for innovation.

## Outcomes

The hackathon was designed to conclude with one or more projects developed during the event.

Potential outcomes included:

- New business ideas
- Collaborative research projects
- Software prototypes
- New Earth observation applications
- Academic–industry collaborations
- Follow-on innovation projects

The organising partners provided opportunities for promising concepts to receive further support after the event.

## Why the Hackathon Matters

The Food Security and Resilience Copernicus Hackathon demonstrated a model for bringing together **space data, multidisciplinary expertise and rapid innovation** around a real-world sustainability challenge.

Rather than treating Earth observation as an end in itself, the event focused on the question:

> **What can we build with this data that makes a difference?**

That approach remains relevant as Earth observation becomes increasingly important to climate adaptation, sustainable agriculture, resilience and environmental decision-making.

## Legacy

The hackathon formed part of the development of Leicester as a centre for **space-enabled innovation and Earth observation applications**.

It brought together an unusually broad ecosystem spanning:

**University research → Space sector → Earth observation → Food systems → Government → Industry → Students → Entrepreneurs**

The event also provided an example of how relatively short, focused innovation programmes can create connections between communities that do not traditionally work together.

Copernicus provides access to extensive environmental data and services derived from satellites, in-situ observations and other sources.

Participants were encouraged to explore how this open data could be transformed into useful applications and services.

Potential applications included:

  • Agriculture
  • Food production
  • Water security
  • Environmental monitoring
  • Climate resilience
  • Logistics
  • Supply chains
  • Resource mapping
  • Risk assessment
  • Insurance
  • Smart cities
  • Decision support

The emphasis was not simply on analysing satellite data, but on turning Earth observation into practical solutions.

Challenge Themes

Participants could select their own challenge within the broad theme of food and water security and resilience.

Suggested areas included:

Smart Agriculture

Using Earth observation and other technologies to improve agricultural decision-making, productivity and resilience.

Logistics and Supply Chains

Exploring how satellite data, logistics technologies and emerging digital infrastructure could improve food supply chains.

Blockchain and Food Security

Investigating potential applications of distributed technologies in food and water supply chains, provenance and resilience.

Smart Insurance

Developing new services that could use Earth observation data to understand environmental risks and support innovative insurance products.

Resource Mapping

Using satellite observations to map, monitor and understand environmental and agricultural resources.

Societal and Technical Challenges

Participants were also encouraged to identify their own challenges relevant to food security, water security and resilience.

The 48-Hour Challenge

The core hackathon took place over 19 and 20 September 2019.

Teams worked intensively over two days to move from an initial problem or idea towards a practical prototype.

The process encouraged rapid experimentation and multidisciplinary collaboration.

Participants combined:

  • Copernicus data
  • Coding
  • Data analysis
  • Design
  • Research
  • Business modelling
  • Storytelling
  • Domain expertise

The objective was to produce something tangible rather than simply discuss potential applications.

Rapid MVP Development

Participants received preparatory training before the main event.

A training session on 12 September 2019 introduced selected teams and other participants to:

  • Agile development
  • Rapid MVP development
  • Copernicus data access
  • Relevant coding libraries
  • Rapid prototyping approaches

This provided teams with a common foundation before the 48-hour event.

The focus on minimum viable products (MVPs) helped participants move rapidly from ideas towards demonstrable concepts.

Knowledge Exchange

The hackathon was designed as a knowledge-exchange activity rather than a conventional coding competition.

It brought together people with different skills and perspectives, allowing technical expertise to be combined with knowledge of food systems, Earth observation, business and societal challenges.

This multidisciplinary approach was central to the event.

A successful solution could require expertise from several different domains, for example:

Satellite data + agriculture + software + business + user needs

rather than technology development in isolation.

My Role

I participated as a mentor, supporting teams during the hackathon and contributing to the wider knowledge exchange around space-enabled applications.

The role involved helping participants think through the practical application of Copernicus data and the development of solutions that could address real-world challenges.

This included supporting teams as they moved through the rapid development process and helping connect technical possibilities with user needs and wider applications.

From Data to Impact

A central theme of the hackathon was the transformation of raw Earth observation data into useful information and ultimately actionable solutions.

The process can be represented as:

Earth observation data → Information → Insight → Application → Impact

Copernicus provides the data infrastructure, but the value emerges when that data is combined with domain knowledge, software, business models and an understanding of user needs.

The hackathon provided a practical environment for exploring this transition.

Food Security and Resilience

Food security is not simply a question of producing more food.

It is influenced by a complex combination of:

  • Climate
  • Water availability
  • Land use
  • Agricultural productivity
  • Supply chains
  • Infrastructure
  • Markets
  • Environmental change
  • Resource availability
  • Human behaviour

Earth observation can provide a powerful perspective because satellites can repeatedly observe large areas of the planet.

This creates opportunities to monitor change, identify risks and support decisions across different scales.

Space-Enabled Innovation

The hackathon demonstrated the potential of space technologies to contribute to challenges far beyond the traditional space sector.

Satellite data can support applications across:

  • Agriculture
  • Food systems
  • Environmental management
  • Climate adaptation
  • Urban planning
  • Logistics
  • Insurance
  • Emergency response
  • Sustainability

The event therefore positioned Copernicus not simply as a source of scientific data, but as an enabling infrastructure for innovation.

Outcomes

The hackathon was designed to conclude with one or more projects developed during the event.

Potential outcomes included:

  • New business ideas
  • Collaborative research projects
  • Software prototypes
  • New Earth observation applications
  • Academic–industry collaborations
  • Follow-on innovation projects

The organising partners provided opportunities for promising concepts to receive further support after the event.

Why the Hackathon Matters

The Food Security and Resilience Copernicus Hackathon demonstrated a model for bringing together space data, multidisciplinary expertise and rapid innovation around a real-world sustainability challenge.

Rather than treating Earth observation as an end in itself, the event focused on the question:

What can we build with this data that makes a difference?

That approach remains relevant as Earth observation becomes increasingly important to climate adaptation, sustainable agriculture, resilience and environmental decision-making.

Legacy

The hackathon formed part of the development of Leicester as a centre for space-enabled innovation and Earth observation applications.

It brought together an unusually broad ecosystem spanning:

University research → Space sector → Earth observation → Food systems → Government → Industry → Students → Entrepreneurs

The event also provided an example of how relatively short, focused innovation programmes can create connections between communities that do not traditionally work together.

## Overview

**DiscovAir** was a personalised environmental-information service designed to
help residents and visitors make better-informed decisions about travel,
outdoor activity and time spent in Greece and Cyprus.

The service combined the user’s location and preferences with atmospheric and
weather information, including air quality, ultraviolet radiation, pollen,
temperature, humidity, wind and cloud cover. It then provided tailored advice
about comfort and health conditions at a selected location. 

I contributed editorial and science-communication work through Design & Data,
helping explain how Copernicus atmospheric data could be transformed into
practical guidance for everyday life.

## The challenge

Environmental conditions can affect travel plans, outdoor activity and personal
comfort, but the data behind these conditions are often difficult to interpret.

A traveller may not want to assess ozone concentrations, particulate matter,
relative humidity or pollen forecasts directly. They are more likely to ask:

- What will air quality be like at my destination?
- Is this a good time to go outside?
- Are pollen levels likely to aggravate allergies?
- Should I take additional precautions in strong sunlight?
- When would be the most comfortable time to visit a beach, park or city?

DiscovAir addressed these questions by combining forecast information with a
user profile, providing advice that was specific to both location and personal
needs.

## The service

DiscovAir was developed by the National Observatory of Athens in partnership
with the Academy of Athens and Evenflow Sprl. It provided assessments of
current and forecast conditions for UV index, air quality, temperature and
pollen at locations across Greece and Cyprus. 

The service was designed for citizens and tourists, helping users organise
trips, days out and outdoor activities through location-specific advice and
alerts. 

It was made available through:

- A mobile application.
- A public website.
- A service portal for tourism operators.
- A service portal for local administrations.

The service portals enabled organisations to access local air-quality
information and weather bulletins for their customers, guests and communities.
[web:259]

## Information provided

DiscovAir combined several environmental variables into advice focused on
health, comfort and travel planning.

| Information area | Example use |
| --- | --- |
| Air quality | Understanding likely exposure to pollution |
| UV index | Planning sun protection and time outdoors |
| Pollen | Managing allergy-related activity choices |
| Temperature | Assessing heat and thermal comfort |
| Humidity and cloud cover | Understanding weather-related comfort |
| Wind and dust aerosols | Supporting activity and travel planning |

The service used CAMS data relating to ozone (\\(\\mathrm{O\_3}\\)), particulate
matter (\\(\\mathrm{PM\_{2.5}}\\) and \\(\\mathrm{PM\_{10}}\\)) and birch pollen. It
also incorporated temperature, relative humidity, cloud cover, wind speed, dust
aerosols and UV-index information. [web:259]

## CAMS contribution

The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (**CAMS**) provides atmospheric
information on air quality, pollutants, pollen and ultraviolet radiation.

For DiscovAir, CAMS supplied atmospheric-composition data that were updated
hourly. These data supported information about current conditions and forecasts
for the days ahead.

The service combined CAMS variables with weather data and individual
health-risk factors to provide personalised recommendations about the optimum
time to visit a location.

Contributed to a Summer Undergraduate Research Experience project investigating the origin and possible identification of unidentified far-ultraviolet spectral lines in hydrogen-deficient white dwarfs.
Radial-velocity discrimination, comparison of stellar spectra, line-list testing and analysis of Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer data.

## Overview

This project investigated unidentified absorption features in the far-ultraviolet
(FUV) spectra of hydrogen-deficient white dwarfs, particularly DO white dwarfs
and PG1159 stars. The work used spectra obtained by the **Far Ultraviolet
Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE)**, a space telescope that observed in the
far-ultraviolet region.

The central problem was that many absorption lines in these stellar spectra had
not been securely identified. Some features could originate in the star’s
photosphere; others could be produced by material in the interstellar medium
(ISM) between the star and Earth. Distinguishing between these origins is an
essential first step before assigning an atomic species or transition to an
unidentified line.

## Research question

How can radial-velocity differences between white dwarfs and the interstellar
medium be used to determine whether unidentified FUV absorption lines are
photospheric or interstellar in origin?

A related question was whether the remaining unidentified features could be
explained by incomplete atomic line lists, including transitions from highly
ionised or iron-group species not adequately represented in available data.

## Method

The analysis used velocity discrimination. In a simplified case, spectra from
two white dwarfs have different separations between their photospheric and ISM
radial velocities.

- A line that shifts with the ISM velocity is likely interstellar.
- A line that shifts with the photospheric velocity is likely stellar.
- Comparing the same feature across stars helps distinguish the two possible
  origins even where a line’s atomic identification is initially unknown.

## Overview

**Keeping Gaia's Memory** is a short European Space Agency documentary about
the investigation of a failed onboard memory module during pre-flight testing
of ESA’s Gaia spacecraft.

Gaia was designed to collect an enormous volume of astronomical observations
while mapping the positions and motions of around one billion stars. Before
those measurements could be transmitted to Earth, they had to be stored safely
in the spacecraft’s onboard solid-state memory. 

When one memory module failed during testing, ESA’s Materials and Electrical
Components Laboratory was asked to determine whether it was an isolated
incident or evidence of a wider manufacturing issue. The investigation used
three-dimensional X-ray tomography to inspect the module internally without
destroying it. 

I contributed script development through Design & Data, helping communicate how
a detailed laboratory investigation can protect the reliability of a major
space-science mission.

## The challenge

Gaia’s scientific goal depended on the dependable operation of many individual
spacecraft components.

The mission’s instruments generated data continuously, but communications with
Earth could not transfer every observation immediately. The spacecraft
therefore needed onboard systems capable of storing observations securely until
they could be downlinked.

During pre-flight testing, one module within Gaia’s onboard “hard disk” failed.
The engineering challenge was not simply to replace it: the team needed to
understand **why** it failed and determine whether similar components might
carry the same risk.

Memory-module failure
→ Cause unknown
→ Potential manufacturing or design risk
→ Non-destructive internal inspection
→ Evidence-based decision for mission reliability

## Gaia mission context

Gaia is ESA’s astrometry mission, designed to create an exceptionally precise
three-dimensional map of the Milky Way.

The spacecraft measures the positions, distances, motions and physical
properties of stars, enabling astronomers to investigate the structure,
formation and evolution of our Galaxy. 

The mission produces a large volume of observational data. Gaia’s payload data
handling system includes solid-state mass memory, which stores data produced by
the onboard video processing units before transmission to ground stations.
[web:292]

Reliable memory hardware is therefore essential: a fault in data storage could
reduce the amount of scientific information recovered from the spacecraft.

## The memory investigation

One of Gaia’s memory modules failed during pre-flight testing.

ESA’s Materials and Electrical Components Laboratory investigated the component
to establish whether the issue was an isolated event or part of a broader
manufacturing problem. Rather than dismantling the module immediately, the team
used a **3D X-ray tomography machine** to examine the hardware internally.
[web:290][web:291]

This approach allowed engineers to see beneath the component’s outer surface
and identify the source of the fault while preserving the item for further
analysis.

## X-ray tomography

Three-dimensional X-ray tomography is a non-destructive imaging technique.

Like medical CT scanning, it uses multiple X-ray views to reconstruct the
interior of an object. For spacecraft electronics, this can reveal internal
features such as:

- Solder joints.
- Wire bonds.
- Cracks.
- Voids.
- Misalignments.
- Delamination.
- Structural defects.
- Manufacturing inconsistencies.

In the Gaia investigation, X-ray tomography enabled ESA engineers to inspect
the memory module’s internal structure and identify the source of the failure
without taking the component apart. [web:290]

```text
Memory module
→ X-ray scans from multiple angles
→ 3D reconstruction of internal structure
→ Identification of the failure source
→ Improved confidence in flight hardware
```

## Why non-destructive testing matters

Space hardware is expensive, tightly qualified and often available in limited
numbers. Engineers need methods that can diagnose faults while preserving the
hardware and maintaining a clear evidence trail.

Non-destructive testing can help teams:

- Identify defects inside sealed components.
- Compare failed and non-failed hardware.
- Investigate potential production issues.
- Support decisions about replacement, requalification or redesign.
- Reduce risk before spacecraft launch.

For Gaia, the test was part of the wider verification culture needed to ensure
that a mission built to operate far from Earth could be trusted after launch.

## My role

I worked as a **Scriptwriter** through Design & Data.

My contribution included:

- Developing the documentary narrative and script structure.
- Translating spacecraft-electronics and failure-analysis concepts into
  accessible language.
- Explaining why an individual memory-component failure mattered to a
  billion-star astronomy mission.
- Supporting the communication of laboratory procedures and technical imagery.
- Connecting microscopic internal evidence with mission-scale reliability.

The editorial objective was to show that space missions depend not only on
spectacular imagery and advanced instruments, but also on careful engineering
work carried out long before launch.

## Editorial approach

The film used a familiar analogy: Gaia’s onboard memory module as part of the
spacecraft’s “hard disk”.

This offered a clear route into a specialist topic:

```text
A familiar problem — failed computer memory
→ A high-stakes context — a spacecraft preparing for launch
→ An advanced diagnostic tool — 3D X-ray tomography
→ A mission-level outcome — protecting scientific data
```

The narrative made the abstract idea of spacecraft qualification tangible by
focusing on a specific object, a specific failure and the forensic process used
to understand it.

## Outcome

The completed documentary was released by ESA in June 2016.

ESA describes **Keeping Gaia's memory** as a film about a memory-module failure
identified during pre-flight testing, followed by a non-destructive
three-dimensional X-ray tomography investigation performed by the Materials and
Electrical Components Laboratory. 

The film formed part of wider ESA communication activity highlighting the
testing, materials research and engineering expertise that support European
space missions.

## Limitations

This project concerned science communication and documentary scripting. It did
not involve conducting the laboratory investigation, manufacturing Gaia
hardware or operating the Gaia mission.

The film focused on one pre-flight component investigation. Spacecraft
reliability depends on a much broader qualification programme, including
environmental testing, radiation assessment, thermal-vacuum tests, vibration
tests, electrical verification, redundancy analysis and system-level
validation.

In the Gaia investigation, X-ray tomography enabled ESA engineers to inspect the memory module’s internal structure and identify the source of the failure without taking the component apart. [web:290]

Memory module
→ X-ray scans from multiple angles
→ 3D reconstruction of internal structure
→ Identification of the failure source
→ Improved confidence in flight hardware

Why non-destructive testing matters

Space hardware is expensive, tightly qualified and often available in limited numbers. Engineers need methods that can diagnose faults while preserving the hardware and maintaining a clear evidence trail.

Non-destructive testing can help teams:

  • Identify defects inside sealed components.
  • Compare failed and non-failed hardware.
  • Investigate potential production issues.
  • Support decisions about replacement, requalification or redesign.
  • Reduce risk before spacecraft launch.

For Gaia, the test was part of the wider verification culture needed to ensure that a mission built to operate far from Earth could be trusted after launch.

My role

I worked as a Scriptwriter through Design & Data.

My contribution included:

  • Developing the documentary narrative and script structure.
  • Translating spacecraft-electronics and failure-analysis concepts into accessible language.
  • Explaining why an individual memory-component failure mattered to a billion-star astronomy mission.
  • Supporting the communication of laboratory procedures and technical imagery.
  • Connecting microscopic internal evidence with mission-scale reliability.

The editorial objective was to show that space missions depend not only on spectacular imagery and advanced instruments, but also on careful engineering work carried out long before launch.

Editorial approach

The film used a familiar analogy: Gaia’s onboard memory module as part of the spacecraft’s “hard disk”.

This offered a clear route into a specialist topic:

A familiar problem — failed computer memory
→ A high-stakes context — a spacecraft preparing for launch
→ An advanced diagnostic tool — 3D X-ray tomography
→ A mission-level outcome — protecting scientific data

The narrative made the abstract idea of spacecraft qualification tangible by focusing on a specific object, a specific failure and the forensic process used to understand it.

Outcome

The completed documentary was released by ESA in June 2016.

ESA describes Keeping Gaia’s memory as a film about a memory-module failure identified during pre-flight testing, followed by a non-destructive three-dimensional X-ray tomography investigation performed by the Materials and Electrical Components Laboratory.

The film formed part of wider ESA communication activity highlighting the testing, materials research and engineering expertise that support European space missions.

Galaxy Facebook: X-ray source population analysis of the Galactic Centre

Undergraduate research project analysing XMM-Newton observations of two Galactic Ridge fields to investigate intermediate-luminosity X-ray sources, compare spectral behaviour across energy bands, and identify candidate variable or transient sources.
XMM-Newton Survey Science Centre / ESA / University of Leicester
XMM-Newton X-ray observation showing point sources and diffuse high-energy emission in a Galactic Ridge field.

Analysed a sample of approximately 30 intermediate-luminosity X-ray sources in two Galactic Ridge fields, comparing source populations, absorption effects and multi-epoch variability to identify candidate transient and high-variability objects.
Reduced and examined multi-instrument XMM-Newton EPIC datasets
Compared source behaviour across five X-ray energy bands
Identified candidate variable and transient X-ray sources
Cross-referenced measured sources with the 2XMM catalogue
Completed an undergraduate research report supervised by Professor Bob Warwick

## Overview

The Galactic Centre and Galactic Ridge contain a dense and complex population
of high-energy sources. X-ray observations reveal emission from compact
binaries, accreting white dwarfs, active stars, supernova remnants, diffuse hot
plasma and more distant background objects seen through the Milky Way.

This undergraduate research project analysed archival observations from ESA's
**XMM-Newton** X-ray observatory. The work focused on discrete sources of
intermediate luminosity in two fields near the Galactic plane: one centred
close to the plane and a second positioned approximately two degrees away from
it.

The project examined source detection, count rates, energy-band behaviour and
variability across multiple observation epochs. It also compared results with
the **2XMM** serendipitous-source catalogue to identify candidate variable or
transient X-ray sources.

## Research question

What are the spectral and temporal properties of intermediate-luminosity X-ray
sources in Galactic Ridge fields, and how do source populations and observed
fluxes differ between a field on the Galactic plane and an off-plane field?

The work considered several related questions:

- Which sources showed substantial changes in flux between observations?
- Which energy bands contributed most strongly to individual sources?
- How did count rates differ between the on-plane and off-plane fields?
- What role might interstellar absorption play in the observed source
  populations?
- Could multi-epoch comparisons identify candidate X-ray transients?

## Scientific context

X-ray astronomy is essential for studying compact and energetic objects that
cannot be understood from visible-light observations alone.

The Galactic plane contains large quantities of gas and dust. This material
absorbs lower-energy X-rays particularly strongly, so observations along the
plane tend to favour harder X-ray sources or nearby objects. Comparing a
plane field with an off-plane field can therefore help distinguish changes in
source density from the effects of interstellar absorption.

Intermediate-luminosity sources are also important because they can include
cataclysmic variables, X-ray binaries, coronally active stars and other
populations that collectively contribute to the Galactic Ridge X-ray emission.

## Observations

The project used archival XMM-Newton observations of two fields in the Galactic
Ridge region.

### Galactic Ridge 1

Galactic Ridge 1 was centred close to the Galactic plane at approximately:

```text
Galactic longitude: 33 degrees 06 minutes
Galactic latitude: 0 degrees
```

The analysed observations were:

| Observation ID | Approximate net exposure |
| --- | ---: |
| `0017740401` | 21 ks |
| `0017740501` | 25 ks |

This field was expected to be affected by substantial line-of-sight absorption
and to contain a comparatively high density of Galactic X-ray sources.

### Galactic Ridge 2

Galactic Ridge 2 was positioned off the plane at approximately:

```text
Galactic longitude: 33 degrees
Galactic latitude: 2 degrees
```

The analysed observations were:

| Observation ID | Approximate net exposure |
| --- | ---: |
| `0017740201` | 15–20 ks |
| `0017740601` | 15–20 ks |
| `0017740701` | 15–20 ks |

Moving away from the plane changes both the absorbing column and the mixture of
objects visible in the field, making the comparison useful for interpreting
population differences.

### EPIC instruments

All observations used XMM-Newton's European Photon Imaging Camera (**EPIC**):

- **MOS1**, a Metal Oxide Semiconductor camera.
- **MOS2**, a second Metal Oxide Semiconductor camera.
- **pn**, a higher-throughput CCD camera.

The observations used the medium optical blocking filter. Combining the three
instruments improved source detection and enabled instrument-by-instrument
comparison of count rates.

## Method

The analysis used Leicester-developed data-analysis tools operating through
command-line Q scripts, including `viewer2.qin` and `sources2.qin`.

### Data reduction

Raw and processed XMM-Newton data products were handled as FITS and HDS/FITS
structures. The reduction process involved preparing data from each EPIC
instrument, inspecting images, selecting source regions and extracting
instrument-specific count rates.

### Multi-band imaging

The source population was examined in five standard XMM-Newton energy bands:

| Band | Energy range |
| --- | --- |
| Band 1 | 0.2–0.5 keV |
| Band 2 | 0.5–2.0 keV |
| Band 3 | 2.0–4.5 keV |
| Band 4 | 4.5–7.5 keV |
| Band 5 | 7.5–12.0 keV |

Comparing these bands made it possible to assess whether a source was
predominantly soft or hard, and to investigate the effects of absorption and
spectral variation.

### Source detection

Candidate point sources were identified using automated extraction procedures.
The analysis considered parameters describing source extent and the fraction
of counts concentrated within the detection cell to distinguish likely
point-like sources from extended structure, noise and diffuse emission.

Source extraction and count-rate measurement used routines including `Jill`
and `Jack`.

### Catalogue comparison

Measured source positions and count rates were compared with archival source
information from:

- The **2XMM** XMM-Newton Serendipitous Source Catalogue.
- The **LEDAS Arnie** service.
- The **HEASARC** archive.

This comparison provided external flux estimates, source designations and
reference values for evaluating differences between epochs.

### Variability analysis

For sources detected in more than one observation, count rates and derived
fluxes were compared across epochs.

Sources with changes substantially larger than their formal measurement
uncertainties were flagged as possible high-variability objects or candidate
X-ray transients. These candidates would require deeper or follow-up
observations for definitive classification.

## Findings

### Candidate variable and transient sources

Several sources showed flux changes that exceeded their formal uncertainties
between observing epochs.

One example was source `168323`, associated with 2XMM J185139.1+001635. This
source showed pronounced variability in the Galactic Ridge 1 data, with strong
emission in the 2.0–4.5 keV band. Its behaviour made it a candidate for further
investigation as a variable or transient X-ray source.

The project identified variability candidates rather than claiming definitive
transient classifications. The available observations provided a limited number
of epochs and were not designed as a continuous monitoring campaign.

### Bright sources and energy dependence

The brightest source identified in Galactic Ridge 1 was source `168300`,
associated with 2XMM J185114.3-000004.

Its EPIC flux was estimated at approximately:

```text
6.1 × 10^-13 erg s^-1 cm^-2
```

The source showed strong emission at higher energies, particularly in Band 5
(7.5–12.0 keV). Hard-band behaviour can indicate intrinsically energetic
sources, substantial foreground absorption, or a combination of both.

### On-plane and off-plane comparison

The Galactic Ridge 1 field generally showed higher active count rates than
Galactic Ridge 2.

This difference was consistent with the expectation that observations close to
the Galactic plane sample a denser population of Galactic X-ray sources while
also experiencing stronger absorption. Soft X-ray emission is preferentially
suppressed by intervening gas and dust, meaning that the observed population
along the plane is weighted towards harder or less absorbed sources.

### Approximate luminosity scale

Using a simple assumed distance of approximately 8 kiloparsecs, comparable to
the distance to the Galactic Centre, the observed intermediate-luminosity
sources corresponded broadly to X-ray luminosities around:

```text
10^32 erg s^-1
```

These values were indicative rather than definitive because source distances
and absorbing columns were not independently determined for every object.
Detailed spectral fitting and absorption corrections would be required to
derive robust intrinsic luminosities.

## Contribution

I completed this research as an undergraduate physics student at the University
of Leicester, working with Leon Hicks under the supervision of **Professor Bob
Warwick**.

The project provided practical experience in:

- Processing space-telescope datasets.
- Working with FITS-based astronomy data products.
- Comparing observations from multiple CCD instruments.
- Assessing X-ray source variability.
- Using archival catalogues and astronomical data services.
- Interpreting high-energy observations in the context of Galactic source
  populations and interstellar absorption.

## Related output

### X-ray source population of the nearby Galactic Centre

**Ryan John McCall Laird**

Undergraduate research report, Department of Physics and Astronomy, University
of Leicester, 16 April 2008.

Supervised by Professor Bob Warwick.

The report documented the XMM-Newton EPIC data-reduction process, source
detection workflow, energy-band comparisons, catalogue cross-matching and
source flux tabulations for Galactic Ridge 1 and Galactic Ridge 2.

## Scientific significance

The Galactic Ridge X-ray emission is produced by a mixture of diffuse
processes and large populations of faint or unresolved point sources.
Understanding the properties of intermediate-luminosity sources helps constrain
the contribution made by Galactic binaries, accreting white dwarfs, active
stars and other compact populations.

This project provided a small-scale observational investigation of that wider
problem. Comparing fields close to and away from the Galactic plane illustrated
how source populations, energy-dependent absorption and observational selection
affect the high-energy view of the Milky Way.

## Limitations

The observations had net exposures of approximately 15–25 kiloseconds per
field. They were therefore substantially shallower than dedicated deep surveys,
limiting sensitivity to faint sources and reducing the ability to classify
short-duration variability.

Other limitations included:

- Detector-edge effects for sources near camera boundaries.
- Differences in effective area and response between MOS and pn instruments.
- Dependence on catalogue cross-calibration when converting count rates to
  physical fluxes.
- Uncertain distances to individual sources.
- Absorption corrections not modelled in detail for every source.
- Limited temporal sampling, which prevents firm classification of transient
  candidates without follow-up data.

The analysis should consequently be interpreted as an exploratory source
population study and as evidence for candidate variability, rather than a
complete census or definitive classification programme.

The Prompt Emission from Gamma Ray Bursts

A final-year MPhys directed reading project at the University of Leicester reviewing the leading theories for the prompt emission of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and assessing how well they stand up against observational evidence. The work culminated in a literature portfolio, a short lecture course outline, a 40-minute lecture and a set of problems for students.
Artist's impression of a gamma-ray burst, showing a narrow relativistic jet launched from a collapsing massive star.
University of Leicester, School of Physics and Astronomy

Produced a structured review of GRB prompt-emission theory, together with teaching materials (lecture course outline, a 40-minute lecture and worked exercises) that translate a specialist research area into an accessible learning sequence.
Literature review spanning the fireball, fireshell and cannonball models
Outline for a six-lecture course on GRB prompt emission
Slides and speaker notes for a single 40-minute lecture
Four exercises covering GRB energetics, source distribution, synchrotron radiation and Fermi acceleration

## Overview

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most luminous electromagnetic events in the
Universe since the Big Bang. They occur at cosmological distances, with an
average redshift of around z ≈ 3 and examples beyond z = 6, yet for a few
seconds they can outshine everything else in the gamma-ray sky.

This project was a directed reading (PA4440 Advanced Study Topic) completed
during the fourth year of an MPhys in Physics with Astrophysics at the
University of Leicester, supervised by Dr Richard Willingale. The aim was to
review the theories that attempt to explain the **prompt emission** — the
gamma-rays that arrive first — and to assess how well each stands up against
the observational evidence.

## The problem

The energy involved is extraordinary. Assuming the emission is isotropic, a
GRB can release up to around 10<sup>47</sup> J within a few seconds. For
comparison, the rest-mass energy of the Sun is about 1.8 × 10<sup>47</sup> J
(E = mc²), and a GRB can emit more energy in ten seconds than the Sun will
radiate over its entire ten-billion-year lifetime.

The physical mechanism behind such an outburst is not fully understood. Any
successful model must explain:

- Huge energy output released over very short timescales.
- Two apparent populations: short bursts (roughly under 2 seconds) and long
  bursts (over 2 seconds).
- Variability down to the millisecond scale, implying a very compact source.
- Non-thermal spectra that are well described empirically by the Band function
  but lack a clear theoretical origin.
- A luminosity so high that the radiation must be relativistically beamed, with
  Lorentz factors above 100, to avoid the compactness problem.

## A short history

- **Vela satellites (1960s):** GRBs were discovered by US satellites built to
  detect gamma-ray pulses from nuclear weapons tests in space. The findings
  were published by Klebesadel and colleagues in 1973.
- **CGRO / BATSE (1991–2000):** thousands of bursts showed an isotropic sky
  distribution, casting doubt on a Galactic origin. The V/V<sub>max</sub> test
  and the log N – log P distribution indicated a cosmological population.
- **BeppoSAX (1996):** the first X-ray afterglows allowed accurate positions,
  optical follow-up and redshift measurements, confirming cosmological
  distances and opening the "afterglow era".
- **Swift (2004) and Fermi/GLAST (launched 11 June 2008):** a new generation of
  missions with better localisation and broader energy coverage. A burst
  detected in April 2009 and followed up with ESO's Very Large Telescope was
  measured at a redshift of 8.2, making it the most distant known object at
  the time.

## Generally accepted ingredients

Despite open questions, nearly all current models share several features:

1. **Relativistic motion** with a Lorentz factor Γ > 100, needed to overcome
   the compactness problem. Relativistic beaming means we see only a fraction
   of the source.
2. **Dissipation** of the energy of the relativistic flow, most likely through
   collisionless shocks.
3. **Synchrotron radiation** from relativistic electrons accelerated in those
   shocks. This agrees reasonably well with afterglow observations, but there
   are concerns about whether it fully explains the prompt spectra.
4. **Jets and collimation**, supported by achromatic "jet breaks" in afterglow
   light curves. Beaming reduces the true energy to around 10<sup>51</sup> erg,
   comparable to a supernova.
5. **A compact object** — a black hole or neutron star — as the central
   engine, most likely formed in the same event.

## Possible engines

- **Long bursts:** the collapse of a massive star (a collapsar or hypernova),
  producing a black hole and accretion disc. This is supported by the
  association of long GRBs with core-collapse supernovae and with
  star-forming regions.
- **Short bursts:** the merger of compact binaries such as neutron
  star–neutron star or neutron star–black hole systems. Direct evidence for
  short-burst progenitors was still lacking at the time of this project.

## Physical processes studied

- **Synchrotron radiation:** derivation from the equations of motion of a
  charged particle in a magnetic field, leading to a power-law spectrum for a
  power-law electron distribution.
- **Cooling breaks:** fast-cooling and slow-cooling regimes and the resulting
  broken power-law spectra.
- **Fermi acceleration:** second-order acceleration (energy gain proportional
  to β²) and the more efficient first-order mechanism at shocks (energy gain of
  about 4β/3 per cycle), which naturally produces a power-law particle
  distribution.
- **Synchrotron self-absorption, Compton scattering and inverse Compton
  scattering**, including the limits imposed by the Klein–Nishina regime.
- **Blackbody components:** evidence that a power law plus a black body can fit
  time-resolved BATSE spectra.

## Theories for the prompt emission

### Fireball model (Rees and Mészáros; reviewed by Piran)

A large amount of energy is released into a compact region, forming an opaque
photon–lepton fireball that expands relativistically. In the internal–external
shocks picture:

- **Internal shocks** between shells of ejecta moving at different speeds
  produce the prompt gamma-rays, so the light curve reflects the activity of
  the inner engine.
- **External shocks** between the outflow and the surrounding medium produce
  the longer-lived afterglow.

The model explains the temporal structure well and is the most widely used
framework, but internal shocks convert only a fraction of kinetic energy into
radiation, and a simple synchrotron spectrum does not fit every burst.

### Fireshell model (Ruffini and collaborators)

This model assumes that all GRBs originate from gravitational collapse to a
black hole. An electron–positron plasma created by vacuum polarisation expands
as an optically thick "fireshell". It is described by only two parameters: the
total plasma energy and the baryon loading, B.

The emission splits into a **proper GRB (P-GRB)**, released when the shell
becomes transparent, and an afterglow phase as the baryons interact with the
circumburst medium. Short bursts divide into "genuine" short GRBs (very low
baryon loading, B < 10<sup>-5</sup>) and "fake" short GRBs (a very low-density
environment). The model also connects naturally to the Amati relation between
peak energy and isotropic-equivalent energy (E<sub>p</sub> ∝ E<sub>iso</sub><sup>~0.5</sup>).
It is one of the few attempts to describe the whole GRB phenomenon in one
framework.

### Cannonball model (Dar, and Heinz and Begelman)

The central engine fires a series of narrow, non-spreading "bullets" that are
quickly decelerated by dense circumburst matter. Pulse widths are set by the
slowing-down time, and the burst duration by how long the engine keeps
emitting bullets.

## Assessment

- The afterglow is reasonably well understood; the prompt emission is not.
- Within the internal shocks picture, the temporal structure is reasonably
  understood, but the **origin of the observed spectrum** remains unclear and
  simple synchrotron emission probably needs modifying.
- The link between long GRBs and core-collapse supernovae points clearly to the
  engine of long bursts, but there is no direct or indirect evidence about the
  progenitors of short bursts.
- How the flow is accelerated and collimated, and what sets its variability,
  remain poorly constrained because the inner engine cannot be observed
  directly.
- Open observational questions include the GRB luminosity function, the burst
  rate as a function of redshift, and how closely GRBs trace star formation.

Overview

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most luminous electromagnetic events in the Universe since the Big Bang. They occur at cosmological distances, with an average redshift of around z ≈ 3 and examples beyond z = 6, yet for a few seconds they can outshine everything else in the gamma-ray sky.

This project was a directed reading (PA4440 Advanced Study Topic) completed during the fourth year of an MPhys in Physics with Astrophysics at the University of Leicester, supervised by Dr Richard Willingale. The aim was to review the theories that attempt to explain the prompt emission — the gamma-rays that arrive first — and to assess how well each stands up against the observational evidence.

The problem

The energy involved is extraordinary. Assuming the emission is isotropic, a GRB can release up to around 1047 J within a few seconds. For comparison, the rest-mass energy of the Sun is about 1.8 × 1047 J (E = mc²), and a GRB can emit more energy in ten seconds than the Sun will radiate over its entire ten-billion-year lifetime.

The physical mechanism behind such an outburst is not fully understood. Any successful model must explain:

  • Huge energy output released over very short timescales.
  • Two apparent populations: short bursts (roughly under 2 seconds) and long bursts (over 2 seconds).
  • Variability down to the millisecond scale, implying a very compact source.
  • Non-thermal spectra that are well described empirically by the Band function but lack a clear theoretical origin.
  • A luminosity so high that the radiation must be relativistically beamed, with Lorentz factors above 100, to avoid the compactness problem.

A short history

  • Vela satellites (1960s): GRBs were discovered by US satellites built to detect gamma-ray pulses from nuclear weapons tests in space. The findings were published by Klebesadel and colleagues in 1973.
  • CGRO / BATSE (1991–2000): thousands of bursts showed an isotropic sky distribution, casting doubt on a Galactic origin. The V/Vmax test and the log N – log P distribution indicated a cosmological population.
  • BeppoSAX (1996): the first X-ray afterglows allowed accurate positions, optical follow-up and redshift measurements, confirming cosmological distances and opening the “afterglow era”.
  • Swift (2004) and Fermi/GLAST (launched 11 June 2008): a new generation of missions with better localisation and broader energy coverage. A burst detected in April 2009 and followed up with ESO’s Very Large Telescope was measured at a redshift of 8.2, making it the most distant known object at the time.

Generally accepted ingredients

Despite open questions, nearly all current models share several features:

  1. Relativistic motion with a Lorentz factor Γ > 100, needed to overcome the compactness problem. Relativistic beaming means we see only a fraction of the source.
  2. Dissipation of the energy of the relativistic flow, most likely through collisionless shocks.
  3. Synchrotron radiation from relativistic electrons accelerated in those shocks. This agrees reasonably well with afterglow observations, but there are concerns about whether it fully explains the prompt spectra.
  4. Jets and collimation, supported by achromatic “jet breaks” in afterglow light curves. Beaming reduces the true energy to around 1051 erg, comparable to a supernova.
  5. A compact object — a black hole or neutron star — as the central engine, most likely formed in the same event.

Possible engines

  • Long bursts: the collapse of a massive star (a collapsar or hypernova), producing a black hole and accretion disc. This is supported by the association of long GRBs with core-collapse supernovae and with star-forming regions.
  • Short bursts: the merger of compact binaries such as neutron star–neutron star or neutron star–black hole systems. Direct evidence for short-burst progenitors was still lacking at the time of this project.

Physical processes studied

  • Synchrotron radiation: derivation from the equations of motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field, leading to a power-law spectrum for a power-law electron distribution.
  • Cooling breaks: fast-cooling and slow-cooling regimes and the resulting broken power-law spectra.
  • Fermi acceleration: second-order acceleration (energy gain proportional to β²) and the more efficient first-order mechanism at shocks (energy gain of about 4β/3 per cycle), which naturally produces a power-law particle distribution.
  • Synchrotron self-absorption, Compton scattering and inverse Compton scattering, including the limits imposed by the Klein–Nishina regime.
  • Blackbody components: evidence that a power law plus a black body can fit time-resolved BATSE spectra.

Theories for the prompt emission

Fireball model (Rees and Mészáros; reviewed by Piran)

A large amount of energy is released into a compact region, forming an opaque photon–lepton fireball that expands relativistically. In the internal–external shocks picture:

  • Internal shocks between shells of ejecta moving at different speeds produce the prompt gamma-rays, so the light curve reflects the activity of the inner engine.
  • External shocks between the outflow and the surrounding medium produce the longer-lived afterglow.

The model explains the temporal structure well and is the most widely used framework, but internal shocks convert only a fraction of kinetic energy into radiation, and a simple synchrotron spectrum does not fit every burst.

Fireshell model (Ruffini and collaborators)

This model assumes that all GRBs originate from gravitational collapse to a black hole. An electron–positron plasma created by vacuum polarisation expands as an optically thick “fireshell”. It is described by only two parameters: the total plasma energy and the baryon loading, B.

The emission splits into a proper GRB (P-GRB), released when the shell becomes transparent, and an afterglow phase as the baryons interact with the circumburst medium. Short bursts divide into “genuine” short GRBs (very low baryon loading, B < 10-5) and “fake” short GRBs (a very low-density environment). The model also connects naturally to the Amati relation between peak energy and isotropic-equivalent energy (Ep ∝ Eiso~0.5). It is one of the few attempts to describe the whole GRB phenomenon in one framework.

Cannonball model (Dar, and Heinz and Begelman)

The central engine fires a series of narrow, non-spreading “bullets” that are quickly decelerated by dense circumburst matter. Pulse widths are set by the slowing-down time, and the burst duration by how long the engine keeps emitting bullets.

Assessment

  • The afterglow is reasonably well understood; the prompt emission is not.
  • Within the internal shocks picture, the temporal structure is reasonably understood, but the origin of the observed spectrum remains unclear and simple synchrotron emission probably needs modifying.
  • The link between long GRBs and core-collapse supernovae points clearly to the engine of long bursts, but there is no direct or indirect evidence about the progenitors of short bursts.
  • How the flow is accelerated and collimated, and what sets its variability, remain poorly constrained because the inner engine cannot be observed directly.
  • Open observational questions include the GRB luminosity function, the burst rate as a function of redshift, and how closely GRBs trace star formation.

## Overview

The **Geostationary Earth Radiation Budget (GERB)** instrument provides dedicated, high-resolution measurements of the Earth's Radiation Budget (ERB) from geostationary orbit. Developed with funding from ESA and NERC, and supported by EUMETSAT, GERB measures the balance between incoming solar shortwave (SW) radiation ($\text{< 4 }\mu\text{m}$) and outgoing longwave (LW) radiation ($\text{>= 4 }\mu\text{m}$).

This project focused on analyzing calibration data from the GERB **Focal Plane Assembly (FPA)** at the Leicester Spectral Calibration Facility (LSCF). The primary objective was to establish reliable relative spectral response curves across all 256 pixels of the detector array spanning a wavelength range of $0.33\text{ }\mu\text{m}$ to $20.0\text{ }\mu\text{m}$.

---

## Instrument & Calibration Setup

* **Focal Plane Assembly (FPA):** Features a 256-element thermoelectric linear array operating at approximately $300\text{ K}$, supported by four Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs). Each pixel ($55 \times 45\text{ }\mu\text{m}$) is coated with gold-black to optimize spectral response.
* **Radiation Sources:** Utilized Quartz Tungsten Halogen (QTH) filament lamps for shortwave measurements ($0.3\text{ to }4\text{ }\mu\text{m}$) and heated ceramic sources for infrared measurements ($4\text{ to }20\text{ }\mu\text{m}$).
* **Reference Detectors:** Calibrated against National Physical Laboratory (NPL) standards using silicon photodiodes for visible wavelengths and platinum-black coated pyroelectric crystals for infrared wavelengths.
* **Vacuum Chamber Environment:** The detector was housed in a vacuum chamber ($\text{< }10^{-4}\text{ mbar}$) with $\text{CaF}_2$ and $\text{ZnSe}$ windows to facilitate precise beam illumination.

---

## Software & Data Processing

To handle complex multi-file calibration datasets, a custom software suite was developed in **Interactive Data Language (IDL)**:

* **Main Program:** Automatically parses data file headers and directory structures to extract vital metadata, including wavelength, window type, and reference detector configurations.
* **Beam Mapping & Ratio Analysis:** Implemented algorithms to map beam profiles using multi-pixel arrays, calculating scaling ratios between reference detectors and GERB $I_1$ and $I_2$ output values.
* **Statistical Filtering:** Processed chopped frame data (ranging from 50 to 200+ frames per cycle) to compute robust means and standard deviations, ensuring high signal-to-noise ratios despite source variability at shorter wavelengths.
